speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to a Bill
Borrowing Authority
whose purpose is to authorize the Government to borrow billions of dollars. If the money was supposed to help low- and middle-income Canadians, I think I would congratulate the Government, sit down, and we could vote on the Budget, so that these measures could be implemented immediately. Unfortunately, the borrowing authority the Government is seeking is certainly not for money that will help people on middle- or low-incomes or people who live in poverty in Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver, Edmonton and other urban centres.
I think we should remember that this is the international year of the homeless. I can assure you, Madam Speaker, that the money the Government wants to borrow will certainly not be used to help this group of citizens but to help the Government's friends, the people who contributed $60,000 and more in the case of the bank failures. Although the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and most Government Members would have us believe that all's well with the world, I would like to recall a study whose findings were published in the newspaper La Presse about a month ago, which showed that poverty still exists in Quebec and the Montreal area and Canada, despite the self-congratulatory stance of this Conservative Government.
First the headlines: More and more people are queuing up for our soup kitchens, an institution that had disappeared altogether and that we had to bring back. Soup kitchens were a creation of the Depression, in the '30s, and in Montreal the only vestige of that time was the Bonneau shelter that was able to help the needy of the entire Montreal area. Unfortunately, non-profit organizations all over Montreal and all over this country are having to set up these soup kitchens.
According to the same study, there are over 500,000 poor people in the greater Montreal area alone, at a time when much is made of the fact that the volume of shares traded on the Montreal Stock Exchange has increased in six years from 3.8 billion to 15.9 billion. I think we should remember that the number of people on welfare has also considerably increased over the last five years. The words inequality and injustice come to mind. When we look at our national unemployment statistics, it does not seem so bad, but when we take a closer look, without getting into greatly detailed analysis, we find that any gains that were made in the economy and job creation were made in Ontario, in the Toronto area, while in regions like the Atlantic Provinces, the West and even in some parts of Ontario and Quebec, in Montreal East and in remote areas, the results have been negative and instead of job creation we have had a reduction in the number of jobs.
Madam Speaker, I have no idea whether the Government Members are fully aware of the three budgets presented by their Government, its attitude and behaviour with respect to senior citizens, its decisions concerning both youth and consumer programs. My colleague behind me happens to be the official critic when it comes to youth programs, and I must

March 12, 1987
Borrowing Authority
say we have witnessed a truly sad performance in this field, nothing but cut-backs and more cut-backs. Yet there is a group of people in Canada who are growing richer, but unfortunately they are always the same people. A moment ago the Conservative Member referred to deficit reduction.
We all agree on that, but why is the Government telling us in the same breath that we have to vote for this measure to borrow more money? Yet at the same time, when dealing with family allowances, the Government saw fit to de-index the first slice of the 3 per cent due to inflation, supposedly to give mothers an opportunity to do their share towards deficit reduction, but this did not stop it from giving wealthier people a $500,000 capital gains tax exemption, a move which will drain $800 million from the public treasury in 1987, from the pockets of all Canadian taxpayers, men and women alike.
I referred earlier to the bankruptcy of financial institutions which cost $1.6 billion to Canadian consumers. Then there was the Prime Minister's stupid decision to transfer a penitentiary from Drummondville to Port-Cartier, a project of $41 million which would have been better spent to help Canadian families or young people who cannot find jobs and could have benefit-ted from programs specially designed for them. Talk about doubling to $15.1 million the expenditures of the Prime Minister's staff. Think about the $2.6 million wasted on organizing the March 1985 Reagan-Mulroney superparty. Remember the trips of the Prime Minister, over $1 million to travel first class all the way at the expense of Canadian taxpayers. Had he acted as a responsible man he would have been the first to set the example instead of urging people to tighten their belts and do without the good things in life. Not this man: he asked others to do what he was not prepared to do himself and, worse still, the Prime Minister and his Government went on a spending spree with the savings of Canadians.
That is something the people simply cannot forgive, and the polls tell the story: 76 per cent have lost faith in this Government. Voters' preferences expressed in polls are particularly significant in Quebec, and the Conservatives can thank their lucky star that the polling firm chose not to put the Rhinoceros Party on the list because they would have gone down ten more points, behind the Rhinos. It is true that the Rhinoceros Party . . . Concerning the Prime Minister, the scandals and everything else that has happened under this Government, 1 think the Rhinos would have been hard put to come up with funnier jokes, because you got to have an imaginative mind to be able to come up with so many scandals and whatever else the Government has experienced lately. The problem is that Canadians end up paying for the mistakes and blunders of this Government.
I might recall that on Monday this week I attended the seminar of the Federation de I'age d'or du Quebec which includes all senior citizens' groups from each and every provincial riding. The elderly people who were there, men and women president of associations of senior citizens, reminded
me about the famous July 26 promises made by the Conservative Government in the riding of Sherbrooke. All the Conservative Members were there. We all remember that at the time, during the electoral campaign, the Prime Minister and all his colleagues made all sorts of promises. Everyone remembers that, at the time-and I have here the press release of the Conservative Party, which shows that I am not making this up-the first priority was to re-establish full cost of living indexation of old age security pensions as of January 1, 1985. This was just a lie because, immediately afterwards, the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and all their Conservative colleagues tried to de-index the first 3 percent of old age security pensions.
Hon. Members will recall what would have happened without the determination, tenacity and energy of senior citizens who said: "Just a minute, Charlie Brown, we have something to tell you; you had better keep your promises." The Prime Minister was forced to admit that he had made a serious mistake and the Conservative Members who had told everyone in their constituencies that the cutbacks were justified realized how wrong they had been, because acting like sheep is never a good idea.
Let us go back to the commitment made on July 26, 1984, in Sherbrooke during the electoral campaign, under Item 4. I can still see the tape showing the Prime Minister with his hand over his heart to show his sincerity and the truth of what he was saying. Item 4 says that the Conservative Government is committed to maintaining the New Horizons Program and to allocating sufficient funds to this program.
That is the promise which the people who were present at the seminar of the Federation de I'age d'or recalled for me. Then, Mrs. Denis, who took the Prime Minister to task on Parliament Hill about the de-indexation of old age security pensions, showed me, with the facts to prove it, that once more, for the umpteenth time, this Prime Minister and this Government had misled senior citizens. After saying that they would allocate sufficient funds, they cut back $4.5 million from the budget of the New Horizons Program.
I trust that the Conservative Members who are here now and all senior citizens clubs in every constituency in Canada, and there is one in each, will remember this deception and the fact that the budget of this program was reduced to $12,127,000 in 1985-86, to $10 million in 1986-87 and to $8.8 million in 1987-88. This adds up to a cutback of $4.5 million after a solemn promise made by all Conservative Members and this Prime Minister to our senior citizens.
I can assure you that people will remember these cutbacks and this behaviour. People will remember. During the next electoral campaign, you will knock on their doors and say: "How are you, I am Mr. so and so, I was your Conservative Member of Parliament". They will reply: "Thank you, but no. You did nothing about the de-indexation of old age security pensions. You were not there to defend our rights when we needed money to organize our cultural, social, recreational or educational activities. You refused to do it and you misled us."

They will say: "As for us, we shall not follow the example of the Prime Minister; we shall not mislead you; we can tell you to your face that we shall vote against you." I have the opportunity to travel to many constituencies in Quebec and the rest of Canada and this has been the reaction of the Canadian population, whether we are speaking about senior citizens, young people, workers or even employers' associations. They are totally dissatisfied with this Government, especially because of its lack of honesty and its failure to achieve anything or to put together a coherent policy to meet the needs of Canadians.
I would also like to touch upon another matter that directly affects Quebecers, and again we know what commitment the Prime Minister and this Government made during the last elections and in the Speeches from the Throne that were delivered here. In all cases it was the same scenario-with one hand on his heart and the other on the Bible, the Prime Minister said he was going to do all that was needed for Quebec to agree to the Canadian Constitution in an honourable and dignified way. So much for the rhetoric. But what are the facts? The proposals put on the table by this Government, Madam Speaker, intended to take away existing rights, important powers that confirm Quebec's distinctive nature and specificity- that of selecting immigrants and managing human resources, immigration-wise.
That was the first time the proposal was put on the table, this Government's proposal not to enshrine in the Constitution, as proposed by the Liberal Party, the Cullen-Couture Agreement which granted powers to Quebec and the right of veto in respect of immigrant selection. But the same may be said about spending powers-the relevant legislation is of great concern to us-borrowing, spending powers. Again this Government, contrary to its commitments, has laid on the table a proposal such that the Quebec Government has not only to turn it down but also to refuse to take part in further constitutional negotiations, including those on native people that will be held over the coming weeks, because the Government will not recognize financial compensation for new social programs.
Here again we have another example of this Prime Minister's and this Government's attitude towards our senior citizens, the sick with respect to whom all Hon. Members will remember the 10 per cent tax on drugs, the young who had some of their programs slashed without added monies to help youth, workers, Quebecers-this Government acted contrary to its commitments, let alone honouring them.
With respect to Quebec matters, I have before me two letters sent to all Members here by the Hon. Marc-Yvan Cote, the Quebec Minister of Transport, concerning those bills. Concerning those two bills, my colleague the transportation critic, the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), has tried to convince this Tory Government and make it aware, to wake
Borrowing Authority

And I could go on, Madam Speaker. My time has expired, but it is my hope, because I do not despair, that some day we will find at least one-I am not asking for 10 or 40, but at least one-Tory Member from Quebec who will wake up and roll up his sleeves, before he looses his seat, and save Quebec's interests.

Madam Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to speak to Bill C-40, an Act to provide borrowing authority. Bill C-40 is a very thin Bill. It is like the policy of the present Government in that it is very thin and contains lots of promises but no action. The Bill asks the House to give to the Tories across the way $3,600 million as may be required for public works and general purposes. Money and plenty of it is looking more and more like the key to everything the Conservative Government hopes to do to recover its popularity.
How can we in the Official Opposition support this Bill when its purpose is to enable the Government to borrow money in order to have the Government carry out its budgetary and general economic policies? As the months go by, it is becoming increasingly and painfully obvious what is wrong with these policies. During the last general election campaign, the Conservatives made a number of promises and in fact over 347
March 12, 1987

carefully articulated promises containing lots of bombast. These promises were made to win the support of Canadians.
The Economic Statement of November, 1984 and the three subsequent Budgets have not in any positive way reflected the promises made by the Conservatives in order to win the support of Canadians. For example, during the last election campaign, the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) made an explicit commitment not to increase income taxes. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) pledged to reform the personal income tax system and said he wanted to make it fairer, more progressive and more productive. I could use the mellifluous tones and the exaggerated and elaborated phrases the Prime Minister used. Elowever, I would suggest that he read the very important admonition of Thomas Paine who said: "Moderation in temper is always a virtue, but moderation in principle is always a vice".
It is clear that in spite of the promises made by the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister, middle and lower-income Canadians have become the victims of the most unfair, regressive and economically stifling tax increases on record brought about by the Budgets of 1985, 1986 and 1987. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) spoke most forcefully, as did our finance critic, in the debate just a few weeks ago. They highlighted a number of issues. They said that the third Budget represents phase 3 of an all-out attack on low and middle-income Canadians. It widens the gap between rich and poor and between the have and the have not regions of the country. These three Budgets with their economic approach to Government gave us the largest tax increase in modern Canadian history. They have gouged $22.8 billion more out of individual taxpayers. This is an average of $2,000 per taxpayer during the tenure of the Government. Compared to that, over the same period of time, corporations are being taxed $2 billion less than they were when the Government took office. Is that what the Minister calls fiscal fairness?
I would like to deal particularly with the cultural sector. It would appear as though the cultural sector has been reaping benefits over the past few months, but when one examines more closely the record of the Government one finds that the picture is not quite so bright. I suggest that we have been duped by the triptych effect that has been used. It has been a real trompe-l'oeil. The masters have been at work creating the kinds of illusions that would make us feel that we have had a great buffet at the arts and cultural table.
Yes, moneys have been allocated to culture from the Department of Communications as they should be since it is the responsibility and role of the Department to build on what has occurred in the past. Let us look to see what exactly has happened and let us examine the dramatic impact the cultural sector has had upon the Canadian economy.
I call to the attention of the House the words of Henry Robertson Luce who said: "The business of business is to take part in the great society", and if I may add, the great Canadian society as long as it will last. Are we being allowed to take part in that great society to the extent that we can and should,
Borrowing Authority
particularly when we are being threatened by the Americanization of Canadian society as we live next door to our allpervasive friends on the American side of the border?
In attempting to measure the contributions of culture to the economy, we must naturally rely on pragmatic definitions of culture. Unfortunately, this ignores all the intangible characteristics which define us as a people. When we think of culture, we often forget to include its economic contributions. We must measure the economic impact of cultural industries on our economy in terms of employment, wages paid, revenues generated and some of the other economic variables. Then we must compare this cultural aggregate with a similar total for the entire economy.
According to the analysis of Statistics Canada, the direct impact of the arts and cultural sector as measured by the Gross Domestic Product, the value of production arising within the geographical boundaries of Canada, was valued at $5.2 billion or 1.7 per cent of the GDP of the entire economy in 1981. It has grown rapidly since then. Arts industry revenues increased by 64 per cent at an average annual rate of 13 per cent between 1977 and 1981. Revenues went from $4.7 billion to $7.7 billion. I point out that it was under a Liberal Government that Canadians flourished and grew in this vital sector of the economy.
With the rapid changes in technology, cultural industries have been able to impact on our lives in considerable measure and with increasing force over the past years. A census of manufacturers' comparison of the 20 largest Canadian manufacturing industries and the arts industry in 1981 revealed that the arts industry was the largest, with employment of 234,280; the sixth largest with salaries and wages of $2.5 billion; and the eleventh largest with revenues of $7.7 billion, equal to the Canadian telecommunications industry.
Let us also look at the impact of certain actions which were taken. Bill C-58 provided revenues of $58 million for Canadian t.v. broadcasters. This has allowed the field of television and broadcasting to grow and benefit. There is a very important program of substituting Canadian advertising for American advertising. For example, when one turns on either an American channel or a Canadian channel showing the same program at 8 p.m. any evening, one sees Canadian advertising. That kind of protection represents 40 per cent of the revenues of a t.v. station. It is very important that that money is staying in Canada. This has been effective in enabling us to be good corporate citizens while at the same time allowing us to promote our own industries.
I could go on and on about the things that have been done to enable the Canadian Gross Domestic Product to grow substantially through the arts and cultural industries. In the Budget of February, 1986, the Minister of Finance announced an allocation of $75 million per year for the next five years for a number of cultural initiatives. subsubtopic: POLLUTION OF ST. LAWRENCE RIVER BY TOXIC CHEMICALS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, loaded with raw sewage and toxic chemicals, the St. Lawrence is a river gasping to survive. An indicator of that is the beluga whale, the numbers of which have dropped from 5,000 to 500 in the last 80 years. The milk of the mother beluga contains so many toxic chemicals that the babies are being poisoned as they nurse, zoologists inform us. The Quebec Minister of the Environment has said: "Like spoiled brats we ignored it, abused it, raped it, poured acid and human wastes into it".
Having realized the error of past practices the Quebec Government promised in November, 1986, to spend $6 billion building over 400 sewage treatment plants in communities along the St. Lawrence River. Can Quebec cope with this problem alone? Some of the poisons dumped in the Great Lakes end up in the St. Lawrence. Ottawa has some responsibilities upstream. Therefore the federal Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) would do well to help restore this magnificent and historic river by matching his words with tangible help instead of just pointing his finger at polluters.

A committee has been set up under the chairmanship of Senneterre municipal councillor Jean Roy.
I attended several meetings with the residents of Senneterre to give them a hand, and I want to underscore the competence of Department of Employment and Immigration Alain Darveau of Hull whose professional advice was of great help, and of Minister Benoit Bouchard who showed willingness to listen to the people.
The committee may recommend one or several options available under the program with a view to helping workers create their own company, acquire new skills, and get $200,000 over the next two years to carry out a realistic study on local economy development and diversification future prospects.
Mr. Speaker, the Senneterre region has real potential for economic recovery.

subtopic: SKEPTICISM ABOUT RESULTS
SKEPTICISM ABOUT RESULTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians have become very skeptical about the Government's intention to change Canada's tax laws because they fear tax reform will not be in their interests since the Government is the only one in the world to allow capital gains from any source to be totally tax-free. Canadians also remember their federal taxes have increased by $1,350 per family per year as a result of taxes imposed by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson).
We now hear the federal Government intends to impose a food tax on Canadian families. Yes, the Government, through the business transfer tax, a hidden sales tax, will be taxing milk, bread, eggs, vegetables, fruit, indeed all groceries. No wonder Canadians are skeptical. What kind of Government would tax the food on our kitchen table? Only a Government that cares not a whit about the people of Canada. Any Government that imposes such a punitive, regressive, and hidden tax on food will be a Government removed from office as soon as the voters have a chance.

subtopic: PEARSON INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT-TREATMENT OF LATE NIGHT ARRIVALS
PEARSON INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT-TREATMENT OF LATE NIGHT ARRIVALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what will it take for the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) to do something about the absolute chaos at Pearson International Airport when hundreds of tired vacationers arrive late at night all at the same time? Indeed, anyone who has had to experience the cramped arrivals area at Toronto Terminal 1 late at night now knows how ineffective is the Government. Hundreds of people suffer, some waiting as long as 90 minutes, unable to find transportation to their homes.
That, in fact, is the key to the problem. Indeed, as late charters land it becomes obvious that the number of taxis and limousines serving the terminal is terribly inadequate. A recent Toronto Star article quotes airport operation manager, Jim Mattock, as saying that airport officials have been aware of the problem for at least two years. Mr. Mattick goes on to say that it may take several months before a solution is in place. This is unacceptable. The Minister of Transport must immediately address a situation which is intolerable for travellers and a disgrace to Canadian airports.

subtopic: ELIGIBILITY OF FORMER ARMED FORCES PERSONNEL
ELIGIBILITY OF FORMER ARMED FORCES PERSONNEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I once again want to raise a matter in this House on behalf of those Canadians, including many retired servicemen who, since January 5, 1986, have had their UIC benefits drastically reduced or eliminated altogether because they had to declare as income their pensions from previous employment.
On December 5, 1986, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) said that those who found subsequent employment and were laid off would be reimbursed
for lost benefits. For almost a year before that statement, those people were told to wait for the report of the Forget Commission. We have had this report but people have still been kept waiting. These people are fed up with waiting for the Government to act. No one at the Employment Centres can tell them when they will receive their money. The Government's treatment of these people is unfair and intolerable.
I call upon the Minister to act now to ensure that those citizens receive their rightful benefits which should never have been taken from them in the first place.

subtopic: CALL FOR ENFORCEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
CALL FOR ENFORCEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in July, 1985, the previous Minister of Communications announced a policy of Canadianization of our bookpublishing industry, a policy welcomed across the country. The Government, in particular decisions regarding publishing takeovers, has not enforced its own policy. The most spectacular exemption permitted was the Prentice Hall acquisition by Gulf and Western, the company with the scorched earth policy. The Conservative Government excused its dereliction of duty on the grounds that it could not implement its new policy retroactively. Or perhaps the Government was scared of forest fires.
It has now been nearly two years since the policy was announced. One case, GLC, has been under review at Investment Canada for over a year. In another sorry example, Gulf and Western was ordered to sell Ginn and Company to Canadian owners which it has not done. It is time the Government threw some cold water on Gulf and Western's scorched earth policy. It should implement its Canadianization policy beginning with disallowing the GLC takeover by Gulf and Western.

This latest agreement will provide funding of up to $85 million from each level of government to assist in Ontario's Countdown Acid Rain Program and reinforce Canada's commitment to cut our sulphur dioxide emissions in half by 1994.
This acid rain agreement, along with the Niagara River clean-up declaration signed earlier this year, demonstrates the

March 12, 1987

More progress has been made by this Government in attacking the problems of the environment within the last two and one-half years than was made in a decade of Liberal administration. OPPOSITION TO PROPOSED ALBERTA LEGISLATION

subtopic: DISPOSAL OF NUCLEAR WASTES-CONCERNS OF MANITOBANS
DISPOSAL OF NUCLEAR WASTES-CONCERNS OF MANITOBANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, an issue of primary concern to my constituents in Manitoba is the disposal of nuclear waste. With the approval of the provincial Government, a research project has been going on in Manitoba for several years. It is being carried out by Atomic Energy Canada Limited with financial support from its American counterparts. The end result will hopefully be the discovery of ways to store nuclear waste safely. This research will benefit not only Manitobans but all Canadians and North Americans.
However, my position, and what I believe the position of the Government of Canada should be, is that any nuclear waste not generated within the borders of Manitoba should not be disposed of in Manitoba. By extension, I believe any province or area that receives the benefits of nuclear power should be responsible for disposal of its own nuclear waste within its own boundaries.
No one denies that the research being undertaken is beneficial, but we must make it clear that once the research is completed Manitoba will not become Canada's dumping ground for nuclear waste.

OPPOSITION TO ACQUISITION OF RANCH LAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the good productive soil given to us here in Canada by an omnipotent God is a sacred trust. We have a responsibility to ensure it is here to grow food for future generations. For too long we have been carelessly placing subdivisions, factories, army bases, and so on, on productive land. If we continue, we will leave a barren Canada for our children. That is why the hundreds of people in the area of the OH Ranch in the Kananaskis country are opposed to the army acquiring prime agricultural land for military purposes, especially when there is an alternative only an hour and half out of Calgary.
Prime agricultural land, a provincial park, the eastern slopes of the Rockies, a habitat for birds and animals, a quiet spot for hundreds of tourists to meditate amidst a beautiful countryside, are all reasons why the Government should refuse even to negotiate for this land.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I had outlined a number of initiatives which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced in the Budget. There is an allocation of $75 million per year for the next five years for cultural industries. I and the cultural industries were very pleased with these initiatives because they support policies and programs that we considered important.
However, these increases do not make up for the cuts made in 1985-86. These cut-backs include $75 million in the CBC; $10 million in CBC high-tech equipment; $1.5 million to the National Film Board; $1 million to the National Arts Centre; and $3.5 million for the Canada Council. Budgetary cut-backs for different cultural projects and programs amounted to $7 million. There are increased radio licence fees and other charges amounting to $22 million. These cut-backs total $121.5 million.

March 12, 1987
Borrowing Authority
In addition, in 1987-88, the Government will place licence fees on telecommunications carriers through the CRTC. As well, in 1987-88, the Government will levy radio frequency fees on government agencies at the federal, provincial and eventually the municipal level. We are told that the Government expects to obtain $10 million from the latter and $6 million from the former. This has left the cultural and communications industry in Canada with losses of $137.5 million.
Let us examine the task force studies, the book tariff and the Budget for 1987. I was quite surprised that the Budget began with the elimination of the book tariff and the Christmas tree tax. A number of task forces and papers were initiated by the former Minister of Communications. They include the Task Force on Broadcasting at a cost of $2.8 million; the Task Force on the National Museums at a cost of $425,000; the Task Force on Funding of the Arts at a cost of $833,000; the Task Force on the Film Industry at a cost of $134,000; the Task Force on the National Arts Centre for $319,000; the Task Force on the Status of the Artist at a cost of $50,000. After we, the taxpayers, have laid out in excess of $4.5 million for all these task forces, what is the result? There has been no action. Added to these expenditures were the millions of dollars spent by the Nielsen task force which, according to the cultural community, were ineffectively, inefficiently and poorly spent. The very meagre consultative process that took place was a non-credible effort.
As well, the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture has tabled its studies and recommendations on federal museum policy and taxation and the arts. That committee recently had its forty-sixth meeting since November.
After spending that $4.5 million and using the committee's time, there has been absolutely no action taken from all of these studies, recommendations and consultations. There is nothing in the Budget of the Minister of Finance respecting the cultural industry. He even failed to indicate that there were representations on the upcoming tax reform. Why were these reports ignored by the Minister of Finance in his Budget Speech? The Government does not believe in delivering on its promises.
Let us examine the book tariff. On June 6, 1986, a customs duty on certain English language books was imposed. Consequently, novels, works of fiction, some periodicals, publications to encourage enrolment in educational institutions outside Canada, and books of printed music reverted to being subject to the legislated duty at the rate of 10 per cent ad valorem under the most favoured nation tariff and the United Kingdom and Ireland tariff.
The amount of duty collected from June 6, 1986, to November 30, 1986, which is the date of the latest available statistics, was $11,142 million. Of the $11 million collected in duty, $9,741 million was collected from the United States; $979,000 was collected from the United Kingdom, which has nothing to do with shakes and shingles; $109,000 from Hong Kong; $85,000 from Japan; $47,000 from Italy, $44,000 from
Belgium and Luxembourg; $37,000 from Spain; $14,000 from West Germany; $14,000 from Switzerland; $2,000 from France; and $1,000 from Ireland. The remaining $69,000 was collected from other countries. This shows the effectiveness of the reprisal against the American action on shakes and shingles.
Finally, after nine months and losses of up to $15 million to the fragile Canadian book publishing industry, the Tories have recognized the errors of their ways and in his February Budget the Minister of Finance removed the ill-conceived, regressive tax on reading. Certainly, the credit for the removal of this tariff must go to Canadian publishers, book sellers and readers who protested long and hard for the tariffs removal. I want to take this opportunity to thank the thousands of Canadians who wrote petitions to me and the House concerning this issue. I want to thank my colleagues for standing up day after day and reading those petitions into the record. The Minister finally saw the light, and I sincerely hope that the removal of this tariff is a clear message by the Government that Canadian cultural industries are not at risk in free trade negotiations.
It is interesting to consider what the Minister will do with the $11 million in new-found money? I am sure he expects to reduce his deficit, but I suggest that he find a way to repay the publishing industry and those who suffered as a result of this ill-conceived measure.
The Minister also found another $1.2 million in his Budget as a result of changing the procedure in reporting the taxes. The new requirement imposed by the Budget for businesses to remit source deductions on a twice-monthly basis will have a negative impact upon large theatres, museums, dance companies, orchestras, and publishing houses. This results in very poor business practice, with more administrative hassles for business, causing much more paperwork. In addition, this measure will squeeze some cultural industries which have uneven or seasonal revenue.
Let us consider the 1987 Estimates. The Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald), in a news release on March 2, 1987, set out the increased amounts of resources to cultural agencies funded by the Government of Canada. The Minister demonstrated creative sleight of hand as the figures she uses are not limited to increases in parliamentary appropriations but include anticipated operating revenues of the individual cultural agencies, leading to the perception of great largess going to these key Canadian cultural agencies. The fact is that most will not even be covered by the inflation rate. It will mean cuts in staff and programs for many.
Let us examine the situation. The Minister's stated amount of increase for the CBC is $50 million, but the actual parliamentary appropriation is $11.6 million. The stated amount of increase for the Canada Council is $5 million, but the actual appropriation is $3.1 million. The stated amount of increase for Telefilm Canada is $3 million, but the actual parliamentary appropriation is $1,522 million. The stated amount of increase for the CRTC is $2 million, but the actual appropriation shows an increase to $2,276 million. The stated amount of
March 12, 1987

increase for the National Film Board is $1 million, but the actual appropriation is $307,000. The stated amount of increase for the National Library is $1 million, but the actual appropriation is $159,000. The stated increase for the National Museums is $19 million, but the actual appropriation is $16,588 million. There was a stated increase of $2 million for the National Arts Centre, but there was actually a loss of $73,000 in the appropriations. The stated amount of increase for the Public Archives is $1 million, but the actual appropriation is $624,000. I hope the Minister found a new abacus to work out these figures.
I believe these figures show the reality of what the cultural agencies will receive.
Since you have signalled that my time has almost expired, let me conclude by saying that I have the deepest conviction that Canadians want to enjoy their environment and express themselves as Canadians. We have lots to say to the rest of the world through our own cultural and creative experiences. I would hope that we would find a way to ensure that those cultural industries would not be put in jeopardy by any action of the House, and every measure taken by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) to add to the increased protection and growth of these agencies, will be well received by all.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to speak to Bill C-40, an Act to provide borrowing authority, under which the Government is seeking an additional $3.6 billion borrowing authority for the 1986-87 budget and $24.3 billion for fiscal year 1988-89.
The first comment I want to make is that, thanks to our sound and well-advised administration, we did manage to reduce the Government's annual need to borrow. When the 1984-85 Budget was tabled the deficit stood at $38.3 billion. I refer you to page 19 of the February Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). The following year, 1985-86, again as a result of our sound administration, the annual deficit dropped from $38.3 billion to $34.4 billion. With the Budget closing at the end of this month we will again post a deficit, but this time down to $32 billion. Next year, due to the elimination of a number of useless expenditures rather than through huge tax increases, we expect to table a Budget of $29.3 billion. A comparison indicates that the financial requirements of the Government over the four years ending in 1987-88 have declined sharply. By financial requirements I mean borrowing needs which are not necessarily the same figures and which do not tally with the deficit figures because the Government has access to certain pension funds and collects money which was
Borrowing Authority
owing. This accounts for the gap between the financial requirements and the deficit of the Government.
The financial requirements amounted to $29.8 billion in 1984-85, and to $30.3 billion the following year. In 1986-87, the year about to end, the financial requirements were reduced by $6 billion through sound administration, and we expect they will continue to decline next year, down to $21.3 billion, the lowest level of Government financial requirements in the past six years.
Canadian taxpayers must be made to understand that the effect of Government decreasing financial requirements is a significant drop in interest levels, to the extent that the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) has acknowledged this achievement by the Government which every Canadian man or woman who has to borrow can appreciate. Earlier this afternoon the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North told the House that the Bank of Canada prime rate was down to 7.28 per cent, lowest ever since 1974. I want to thank my colleague from Winnipeg North because, even though he is a socialist, in some cases he can read figures when they are not too complicated.
Madam Speaker, for the benefit of all Canadians, it might be a good idea to explain what we intend to do with the borrowed money. This morning the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) raked us over the coals about the use of these funds. Out of budgetary appropriations totalling $122 billion, $57 billion of the expenditures will be in the form of small cut-backs for poorer Canadians. We are going to allocate $57 billion to social affairs, unemployment insurance, youth, the elderly, and needy Canadians. And another, in fact the greater part of our Budget, thanks to the poor management of the previous Liberal Government, will be allocated, all $28 billion, to servicing the national debt, a cumulative deficit of about $300 billion.
Meanwhile, Madam Speaker, the Liberal Party's big guns have been criticizing our fiscal policy and the message we gave Canadians in February, and today they are criticizing our borrowing requirements. One minute they ask us to send cheques to the neediest in this country and the next, they are up in arms about our borrowing authority Bill and the $24 billion involved.
I was listening to the Official Opposition's finance critic, a colleague from Quebec, the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau). I would like to ask him why his assessment of our Budget is so different from the standards he should be applying, as a former director and president of one of Quebec's major banks. It seems to me that he of all people should be far more perceptive in his reactions to the Budget and Budget speech. He is clearly reacting in a very partisan manner. That seems to be his style since he came back to politics. The Hon. Member was always very good at making a profit for his employers when he was in the private sector, but when he entered politics and became a member of provincial and federal cabinets, he became an expert at making deficits. We saw this when he was with the Quebec Government and we

see it today. He has been consistently negative about this Budget.
I would like to ask the Hon. Member, since he is criticizing our message, why, as a Quebecer, he did not rise in the House when we debated the plan to set up an international banking centre in Montreal? I was sitting on the same committee as the Hon. Member, and I did not see him intervene in any significant way to urge that an international banking centre be established in Montreal. His silence was heard across the country. Perhaps his political ambition extends beyond the job of lieutenant to the present Leader of the Liberal Party. Who knows, Madam Speaker.
I also would like to know why the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides was so careful to say nothing about the F-18, a one-billion-dollar contract that is to be administered in the province of Quebec. We never got a clear and straightforward statement from him on this question.
And since he is such a good critic of our Budget, 1 would also like to ask him why, except when he had some specific question in mind, he never referred to our policy to provide, on a long-term basis, for a viable shipbuilding industry in the province of Quebec.
Notwithstanding a number of problems which many experts thought it would be impossible to resolve, our Government has been able to revive the shipbuilding industry in the province of Quebec and I am referring to the shipyards of Versatile Vickers, those in Sorel and those in my own riding in Lauzon, the former Davie shipyards now being managed by Marine Industries. Why did we never hear the Hon. Member from Laval-des-Rapides on a project that is having an economic impact worth over one billion dollars on the three shipyards I referred to?
I would have liked to have heard the Hon. Member comment on the appropriateness of the Government's decision to award a $135 billion contract to Marine Industries for the construction of a second ferry, to award two contracts for refitting some of our destroyers and to award a $196 billion contract to Lauzon for building one and a half frigates, which adds up to $471 billion in federal contracts for Quebec. I would have liked to have heard him voice his support for the two additional $70-billion contracts for repairs to two other Canadian Navy ships. I would have liked to have heard him give his opinion also on the recent financial implication, to the tune of $35 million, of the Canadian Government, the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, to allow for the transaction between Marine Industries and the Levis shipyards. I would also have liked to have heard his comments on the approval by the Canadian Government of a $50-million dollar investment, $30 million for the development of additional capital investments and $20 million for specialization. Also, $50 million were given by the Quebec Government to modernize the three shipyards I just mentioned.
I would also have liked to have heard him express concern for the finalization of the transaction between Marine Industries and the Government of Canada and the former
Versatile shipyards, for which the two governments, Quebec and Ottawa, decided to guarantee $50 million each with respect to the deficit over the next two years.
And, finally, I would have liked him to get involved on the awarding of another $ 196-million contract for an additional frigate and a half to the Sorel yards, for a grand total of $1.22 billion. But the senior Liberal spokesman for the Province of Quebec never showed any concern for those matters.
I would also have liked the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) to share his views with us, since he can hardly express the views of his party, because he would have had one opinion, that of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg- Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) who is against bilateral talks with the United States. He would also have had another opinion, that of the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston), who is for bilateral talks with the Americans, while the critic, who sits to the right of the Leader of the Liberal Party, has not yet committed himself on a matter of such significance for this country and for the Province of Quebec. I say for this country because we export $95 billion worth of goods to the United States, Madam Speaker. This accounts for 30 per cent of our jobs. And the talks are aimed, first at keeping that market, and second at developing it so that we can sell more Canadian goods and services to those 240 million Americans. We have not heard him. The Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides has remained silent on that matter.
I will hurry. I would have liked to have heard him, Madam Speaker, on the lumber issue. He remained silent.
I would have liked to have heard him about Bill C-22, which deals with the drug industry and the location in Montreal of high-technology industries, industries that create plenty of jobs, industries that, since the announcement of our Bill, have decided to invest $700 million in the City of Montreal, Madam Speaker. Fifty per cent of the pharmaceutical companies' new investments will be in the City of Montreal, in the Province of Quebec, but we never heard anything from the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides, who is currently dabbling at launching the Quebec federal organization for the next election. He would do better to make representations here in this House and do his share to improve the lot of Canadians.
Madam Speaker, I will also add a few comments on the position taken by the Leader of the Opposition and perhaps even on his statements. It is not by accident that I began with the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides. The Leader of the Opposition has tried to voice a few comments on the budget speech and our borrowing needs. I should say to the Liberal Leader that before taking position on a budget of so many billions, that is $122 billion, and before giving us some advice on the matter, I wonder if it would not be advisable for him to look after the $5 million deficit which his party is unable to pay back week after week, month after month. I think that would be more important. And when the Liberal Leader is telling us that we are overburdening Canadian taxpayers, he should realize he is living in a democratic system and ask
March 12, 1987

himself how it will be if ever he returns to power 40 years from now? What would be the situation if we listened to his philosophy because today, two years or maybe two years and a half before the next federal election, he is already bearing down on his candidates asking them to collect funds and send 50 per cent to the national organization, something which has never been done before within the Liberal Party. If he is now taxing his own candidates, how will he be taxing the Canadian people later?
Finally, before I hear him give us some further advice, he who was elected to this House in 1962 and appointed minister in 1965, I am still referring to the current leader of the Liberal Party, who was a member of a Government responsible for the $240 billion debt with which Canadian are faced, I will tell him that it is to pay this debt and the interests on this debt that today we have to adopt a legislation calling for $24 billion in borrowing authority. This is partly due to the incompetence of this Liberal Leader who sat in the House for 20 years and did absolutely nothing except increase our indebtedness year after year.
Finally, Madam Speaker, before listening to the negative comments of the Leader of the Liberal Party on our legislation, I think he would be well advised to check the position of the rank and file of his own Party concerning the cruise missile issue and the stand taken at its last convention in November 1986. At that convention, his Party proposed an extraordinary child care project which would cost Canadian taxpayers $11.2 billion a year, Madam Speaker.
Before he starts commenting on our budget, I should like him to tell us how he is planning to finance his own Party's proposal of a child care system which would cost Canadians $11.2 billion a year; I should like him also to explain to the House how he is planning to set up a guaranteed income program for all Canadians. Such programs are good- socialists are experts at that-but I think it is a good idea first to find out how much they will cost. I should like, therefore, the Leader of the Liberal Party to explain to us how he is planning to finance this new guaranteed income concept. 1 should like him to tell us in his masterly fashion what costs are associated with the recommendations made at the November 1986 Liberal convention.
Finally, Madam Speaker, I should like to comment on some of the statements made by the Leader of the Socialist Party concerning our legislative program and our economic message of February 1987. First of all, before speaking of a country's finance, the leader of the Socialist Party should explain to us why the financing of his own Party is questioned in a decision rendered in July 1986 by Hon. Justice John White, of the Supreme Court of Ontario, indicating that the fund obtained by the unions under the Rand Formula-the Rand Formula compels employers to collect money every week from the pay cheques of unionized and non-unionized employees alike. But all these contributions received from the union are used to enrich the Socialist Party. But Mr. Justice White ruled that the union could not use for purposes other than those of the

union the amounts thus collected by the unions by payroll deductions of non-unionized employees.
I mentioned this in the House on a number of occasions, Madam Speaker, and Socialists sitting on opposite benches should listen to me first and tell me where they stand on this particular issue, and if they want to enlighten us about the budget of our Government, they should explain first to the Canadian public why they use these funds illegally obtained to finance their own Party.
Since they keep bragging about the honesty and the openness of their Party, I should like them to tell me why- and here I quote the Minister of Justice who directed in vain this question to the Leader of the Socialist Party-they are using stamps provided by Parliament, meaning Canadian taxpayers' money, to send their political literature to the St-John-East Riding in Newfoundland. On this issue, again, the Leader of the Socialist Party did not know what to say. Therefore, before he starts questioning our budget, I should like him to explain his position on this issue.
Finally, I would like to say something to socialists throughout the world and ask them whether they are aware of the fact that the leader of the socialist party in this House gets $101,700 a year and that he has not only refused to accept the pay cut agreed to by the Prime Minister of Canada and the Cabinet Ministers of this Conservative Government but he has also negotiated for a chauffeur and a car.
Before trying to tell us what to do, and I understand that my time is running short, Madam Speaker, they should think about those matters and about how they use Government services improperly. They are very silent today, which is surprising. They should explain their position to us and think about the White ruling and about Professor Lavigne, who discovered the NDP financing scandal. Then, they can comment on our budget. For all these reasons, Madam Speaker, 1 hope that the Members of this House will support this borrowing authority bill so that the neediest people in Canada, whom we are always trying to protect, will be able to receive their money in good time.

I wish to correct an impression which the Hon. Member may have left with anybody who happens to read a copy of his speech. The decision of Mr. Justice White that the Member talks about was not a decision regarding the use of union dues for political contributions, it was a decision which strikes at the ability of unions to do almost anything for their members. If that decision is carried to its logical conclusion, unions would be precluded from urging their members to support a better pension plan, or from urging their members to defend the universal medicare or hospital insurance plan. That is what that decision would result in. The unions are appealing that decision. They are quite hopeful, as are we, that if the

March 12, 1987
Radio Act
decision reaches the Supreme Court, it will reject that decision.
Insofar as unions contributing to political Parties are concerned, whether it be our Party or any other, I wish to make it clear to the Hon. Member, in case he is not aware, that every union which makes a contribution on the part of its members to the New Democratic Party gives every member the opportunity to notify the treasurer of the union that he or she does not wish a contribution made to our Party on his or her behalf. That is a great deal more than offered the shareholders of banks, insurance companies, or any of the large corporations which contribute to the Liberal or Conservative Parties. They do not ask their shareholders whether they wish to make a contribution, they just do it. If the Hon. Member wishes to look for justice, that is where he should look.
I rose because during the course of his speech, the Hon. Member referred to a question I asked the Hon. Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) during Question Period. I pointed out, and I would not wish to hide it even if I could, that the prime rate of interest as established by the Bank of Canada has come down 5 percentage points from the day that this Government took office until today.

Madam Speaker, I rise for the third time to address Bill C-3, an Act to amend the Radio Act. I have attempted to bring to the attention of the House some of the serious concerns that are found in this not too well conceived piece of legislation.
To return to the issue and reset the stage, it would be useful to set the context of the administrative actions which take place under the Radio Act and relate to this amendment. We are talking about an amendment to the question of charging fees for radio licences, that is, the licences which are authorized and given to users of various types of radio and dispatch services for police, ambulance, fire, taxis, cement trucks, et cetera. It also includes paging services, cellular radio,
March 12, 1987

microwave radio, that is, transmission of data and broadcasting information from city to city, satellites, and radio locations. In other words, radar, and all those things.
Mr. Gordon of the Department of Communications outlined to the Senate committee the issues covered by this particular Bill. He notes that the costs of spectrum management are recovered from users through licence fees.
In 1984, and subsequently in the spring of 1985, the Government announced that it intended that the cost of these services be recovered from the licence users. Accordingly, in the fall of 1984, the fees for licences were significantly increased, and they are now at a level where they cover all of the costs including departmental overhead for these activities of the spectrum. It is important to note that all the activities presently are covered. There is no cost to the Government. Therefore, what we are looking at is a new way to tax the users of radio services, and to find offsetting funds that go to the general consolidated revenues of the Government. It is another way for the Minister to take tax money out of the pockets of users of this service, who for many years have not had to pay this fee.
There is one concern, with which I would agree, in the thinking of the ministry and the Minister in the placing of this tax, and that is with respect to competition in the private sector. By placing private users and Government users on the same footing, Bill C-3 will reduce one advantage previously enjoyed by Government, namely, the exemption from radio licence fees. For example, when a Crown corporation like Petro-Canada communicates through radio frequencies with its drilling rigs, the corporation will not be assessed licence fees on the same basis as would a private oil company, such as Texaco or Shell. I think that is only fair. Our legislative committee was told by Cantel Inc. that the Crown corporation known as AGT, Alberta Government Telephones, has been exempt to date from paying licence fees with respect to its cellular telephone operation. Yet private firms competing with the Alberta Government Telephones in the same cellular telephone market have been paying radio licence fees. Bill C-3 will eliminate this particular cost advantage enjoyed by Crown companies like AGT. I think that is significant.
The other aspect is that there are no caps on the fees to be charged. As I said, we have just found a new way to tax and pay off the deficit. I do not think this is the fairest way of doing that. The Government tells us that the purpose of Bill C-3 is to allow full recovery of the costs incurred by the Department of Communications in monitoring the spectrum. There is nothing in this Bill which provides that the Government is limited to the recovery of those costs, and no more. Given the track record of this Government for charging fees at every opportunity, it remains to be seen if this Bill will prove to be more than a cost recovery vehicle.
Further, although the Government indicates that the fees to be charged Government users under this Bill will be calculated
Radio Act
on the same basis as the fees already assessed to private users, I wish to point out that Bill C-3 does not so provide. Rather, the drafters of Bill C-3 seem content to allow the regulations to stipulate that the fee assessment will be the same. This means that even if Bill C-3 is passed, there is no absolute assurance that Government and private sector users of the spectrum will be assessed licence fees calculated on the same basis, for the Government could still amend the regulations to require one class of user, be it Government or private sector, to pay higher fees. I think that is a real conundrum. Shame. I can only hope, therefore, that the Government will ensure that the regulations are consistent to ensure this equality of treatment of which it is so proud. The Government seems also, to want to use this as a theory for the Bill.
Let us see what the provincial Governments have to say. We are talking about a Government that has wonderful relations with all the provinces, with a new wonderful dialogue going. Do provincial Governments agree with the federal Government on this cost recovery equal payment procedure? I am glad that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister is listening so carefully. Maybe she would like to propose an amendment before I get through.

The Province of Saskatchewan objects to the passage of Bill C-3 on the grounds that it would amount to the federal Government taxing the provincial Governments. In a letter to the current Minister of Communications for Canada dated November 3, 1986, the Hon. Gary Lane, Minister of Communications for Saskatchewan wrote:
Dear Ms. MacDonald:
I am writing in response to your letter of August 13, 1986, in which you confirm the intention to eliminate radio license fee exemptions for Provincial Governments and Crown agents.
While I do appreciate advance notice of your Department's intention, I must respond by stating that the Government of Saskatchewan is opposed to such a gesture by the Federal Government, a gesture which nets approximately $1 million from Saskatchewan.
Isn't the province having some financial problems? This will certainly help.
As you are aware, Saskatchewan is not a participant in the Reciprocal Taxation Agreements. Our non-participation stems from the debate surrounding the taxation of Governments by other Governments. While radio license fees are not taxes, similar arguments about Governments charging fees to each other can be invoked.
I hope the Government resolves that problem when it talks to the province.
While deficit reduction is an important endeavour, shifting the deficit onto a different level of Government is not a true solution to the problem. This is especially true when the intended solution will likely lead to an increased administrative effort for both levels of Government. Surely it would be better to reduce the bureaucracy in this country rather than find yet another way to add to it.
I would like to say that your Department's intention seems contrary to the spirit that has led to many instances of the provinces and the federal Government working in harmony together. Removing the established Provincial fee exemptions is hardly in keeping with the spirit of federal-provincial co-operation.
With this letter, 1 wish to put the Government of Saskatchewan on record as being opposed to your stated intentions on this matter.
I cannot lend support nor comply with any plan to collect radio licence fees from this or any other province.
Let us see what the figures are, and I would hope that there has been no over-expectation reflected in the Minister's calculations for Saskatchewan. I would say that the Minister's figures are in line because the major amounts will be collected from the department of northern Saskatchewan which will pay $2,705. The Departments of Parks, Tourism and Renewal Resources will pay $142,728, Energy and Mines will pay $1,606, Highways and Transportation will pay $60,944; the Department of Education will pay $7,262 and Government Services will pay $1,661. I see that the Department of Education will be paying as well. Today's youth have so many problems that we need every cent possible for education at the provincial level. I do not like to see additional moneys taken from the educational envelope of any Government. The Department of Justice will pay $4,282, the Highway Traffic Board will pay $4,155; Supply and Services will pay $1,012; Communications will pay $1,276 and others will pay $4,690 for a grand total of $232,321. The Saskatchewan Power Corporation will pay $59,445; forest products will pay $1,662 and the telecommunications network will pay $645,522. I hope the people of Saskatchewan will not have their rates raised but it looks like they will.
Let us go on to see what Prince Edward Island had to say. Everyone from coast to coast loves the Tories. The Minister responsible for communications for the Province of Prince Edward Island made the same point in his letter of December 16, 1986, to Mr. Andre Reny, Clerk of the Senate Committee on Transportation and Communications. The letter reads:
Your telex to Premier Ghiz regarding provincial representation on Bill C-3 "An Act to Amend the Radio Act" has been passed to me for reply.
The provincial government will not be making representation in person to the Standing Committee; however, I wish to place on record the contents of a letter I earlier sent to the Minister of Communications, Hon. Flora MacDonald, on the proposal of the Government of Canada to remove radio license fee exemptions for provincial governments and Crown Agencies and the preferential fee treatment currently afforded municipalities.
We have now heard the word "municipalities" for the first time. I know the Minister has promised faithfully that municipalities will not be charged for now. The letter to which the Minister referred reads as follows:
"I am in receipt of your letter dated August 13, 1986, advising me of your government's intention to remove the radio license fee exemptions for provincial government and Crown Agencies and the preferential fee treatment currently afforded municipalities effective April 1, 1987.
Since receiving your letter, officials in my Department have held discussions with both their counterparts in the other Atlantic Provinces and officials in your Department in an attempt to determine the full impact to this Province and Region of this proposed action by your government. The financial impact of the policy change on this Province appears to be substantial-i.e. $22,874 for Provincial Government departments and $2,169 for Municipalities annually.
I suppose they do not know that municipalities will not be taxed, according to the Minister.

I think that theme is consistent across the land.
1 have here another letter, from the Government of Newfoundland which has added its objection to the passage of Bill C-3. It is dated December 12. The Government of Newfoundland and Labrador has stated the following:
While we do not wish to appear before the Committee, on behalf of the Government of Newfoundland 1 wish to express my objection, in principle, to Bill C-3, "An Act to Amend the Radio Act".
By itself this initiative has relatively little financial impact on our Province. However, coupled with other Federal initiatives which have also transferred some degree of financial burden to the Province, the impact is significant.
That letter is signed by James Russell, a Minister in the Government of Newfoundland.
In both Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island, the impact of this Bill will be important because these are the regions of Canada with economic and unemployment problems. The Government's promise of jobs, jobs, jobs has not been kept in that part of our land. It is strange that our actions do not always follow the intent of our words.

The hydro company will pay an additional cost of $25,296. We are talking about a fair amount of money.
In Prince Edward Island, the Department of Highways and Public Works will be paying $9,484; Community Affairs will be paying $2,008; the Department of Agriculture will be paying $2,720 and the Department of Education will be paying $7,000. I would like to know why that fee is so high. I would strongly recommend that the Minister of Education in Prince Edward Island re-check that figure. It seems to be way out of line compared to all the other charges to provincial education
Radio Act
departments. I alert the Minister, the Parliamentary Secretary and the Government of Prince Edward Island to that figure and would ask them to check it out.
Representatives of the Department of Transportation of the Province of New Brunswick appeared before the House legislative committee on Bill C-3 with a very interesting and different complaint. The Hon. Robert McCready, Minister of Communications for New Brunswick, appeared before the Senate Committee on the same matter. New Brunswick advised that it has recently constructed a province-wide communications network which would be in part used for emergency communications. This was done at the federal Government's suggestion and the federal Government made significant capital contributions to its construction. Bill C-3 would require New Brunswick to pay radio licence fees to operate this service. New Brunswick views this as being a penalty for having responded to the important federal initiative of setting up emergency-measure operations. It is strange that when the Government asked them to set these operations up it did not indicate that it would tax them in this way.
New Brunswick also makes the point that the greatest part of the radio licences required by the province are used to ensure the safety and well-being of its residents. New Brunswick advises that radio licences used by its Department of Justice are for the provincial highway patrol. Its Department of Transportation uses radio frequencies for highway construction and maintenance. Its Department of Natural Resources needs radio frequencies for the maintenance of forests and wildlife.
The point is that the Province of New Brunswick, as an entity, is not the user which benefits from the use of radio frequencies. It is the residents of the province who are the beneficiaries. Those people already pay taxes and the cost of the radio spectrum management is already covered in those taxes. This is their major complaint. They say this is a shift of the tax burden from the federal Government to the provincial Government and it is unacceptable. They are echoing once again what I have read into the record from all other provinces.
They say the co-operation of the Department of Communications in providing detailed information is appreciated. The Minister of Communications confirmed the Government's intentions concerning this matter in a letter to the provincial Minister. That Minister is very concerned with the increasing trend by Government towards cost recovery as a budget control measure. He feels this is governed in general by the rationale that if a service exists for the benefit of a particular user, then the appropriateness of having that user pay in part or in whole for the cost of providing the service can be considered. If a particular user cannot be identified, efforts are directed towards controlling increases in the cost of providing the service. It is at times difficult to determine the particular user for whom a service exists, therefore you cannot target

where the fee is going. That Minister feels very strongly that we should not be asking his province to pay a licence fee.
The federal Department of Communications apparently identified the provincial Government as the user of the service represented by the radio licence. However, the greatest part of the radio licences required by the province are used to ensure the safety and well-being of its residents. He refers to emergency systems which are in the interests of all Canadians. He feels the imposition of a user-fee reflecting this rationale amounts to an unacceptable tax transfer from the federal Government to the provincial Government. I would like to look at Ontario. The Hon. Ed Fulton, Minister of Communications, also opposes passage of the Bill. He wrote his federal counterpart on February 9, 1987, and said that he urges the Government to reconsider removal of the radio licence fee exemption for provincial Governments and Crown agencies. He says if the Bill is passed in its present form steps should be taken to minimize its adverse effect on public services. While he understands the Government's desire
to place such services on a user-pay basis, the use of the radio spectrum by Ontario government users is not revenue-producing. It is used to provide essential services to the public, including emergency services. The reasoning which has led the Government to support the exemption of municipalities from the fee requirement is fully applicable to those similar services provided by provincial Governments. He recognizes there is a need to address the anomalies created when operations in one jurisdiction pay for services while similar operations in another do not, when Crown corporations offering services in competition with the private sector are exempt from fees paid by their competitors. Even Ontario feels that where there is competition it is not a bad idea, which is what I said earlier. I felt that was fair in that instance. Mr. Fulton points out that it should be possible to deal with those few major anomalies without affecting the whole spectrum of public service.
The proposed fees will have a substantial impact on the telecommunication budgets of provincial government programs providing important services. In some cases this will amount to 10 per cent of the budget. Total cost to the Government of Ontario is expected to amount to nearly $1.4 million. If the Bill is passed in its present form he urges ministry officials to meet with their opposite numbers in the provinces to discuss issues raised by the current fee structure and consider alterations. He also urges that implementation of the Act be delayed until such discussions have taken place. We are not doing that because we do not need any more dialogue. We have had plenty. However, Mr. Fulton feels that federal-provincial cooperation should serve to minimize the impact of these changes to the public benefit if that dialogue is entered into.

I have a fairly lengthy letter to Russell MacLellan, M.P., Chairman of the Legislative Committee, from the Hon. Gary Doer. It reads:
I would like to bring to your attention this Government's concerns with respect to the amendment to the Radio Act proposed in Bill C-3.
This Bill will have the effect of imposing new costs on taxpayers and telecommunications users in this Province. We estimate the total impact to be in the neighbourhood of three-quarters of a million dollars, based on current rate schedules.
There has been no consultation with provincial governments before tabling this bill, even though its purpose is to effect a cost transfer to provincial agencies for services previously provided cost-free by the federal Department of Communications.
The imposition of radio license fees on Crown agencies will create financial barriers to the installation of the most effective and flexible communications facilities for public services operated by government departments and Crown agencies.
The safety of any number of public services could be compromised by the need to limit the use of radio services in order to keep expenditures for access to the radio spectrum within budgetary limits. Of greatest concern is the fact that public emergency support services, particularly those related to fire fighting and emergency preparedness will be required to restrict access to the radio spectrum and/or tax their limited budgets to pay license fees.
The federal Minister of Communications has made temporary commitments to limit the application of license fee regulations to municipal services.
However, this exemption is not permanent, and does not cover a number of public safety and emergency services such as fire and rescue services operated by northern communities too small to have municipal status, forest fire fighting equipment operated by provincial departments of Natural Resources, or services used by provincial Emergency Measures Organizations. Canada will be less well prepared in times of need if agents of Her Majesty which are using the radio spectrum for safety, emergency preparedness, or rescue services are charged license fees on the same basis as commercial undertakings.
