speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today to speak at third reading stage of Bill C-3, an Act to amend the Radio Act. This Bill will enable the Government to collect roughly $10 million more a year for the regulation of the radio spectrum. Fees are already being collected from municipalities. This will enable the Government to collect fees from provinces and provincial Crown agencies as well. Municipalities are not covered because they are already being charged fees, albeit lower than those charged commercial enterprises. Those fees are increasing and municipalities will be concerned that they will be in for further fee increases

March 12, 1987
Radio Act
when this Bill is passed. Last year the fees charged to municipalities for radio spectrum were more than doubled from $400,000 to $900,000. We are told that if the full fees were charged they would amount to $3.3 million. There are 3,200 municipalities which pay and have to be worried about what they will be charged in the future.
There is one good argument for this Bill that private corporations which came before us pointed out. There are some instances in which they are competing with a service provided through a provincial Crown agency which is exempt from radio fees. The radio fees are not a significant amount of their business expenses but, nevertheless, one can understand the worry of unfair competition when one company providing a service has to pay a fee which another company does not have to pay. However, I remind the House that these are very, very small exceptions. In the vast majority of cases in which the Government intends to charge these fees, they are not for commercial enterprises but, instead, for a service being provided by a provincial government or provincial Crown agencies which are, in some cases, extremely essential services.
This is a proposition for the federal Crown to impose a tax on the provincial Crown. In the end the taxpayer pays. The amount of money saved by the federal taxpayer will have to be paid by someone, which means that the provincial governments will have to increase the taxes they charge. They, of course, have at least as many financial difficulties as has the federal Government. The poor ordinary taxpayer wonders what we are up to. While the Government is making a very laudatory attempt to collect $10 million more in order to bring spending under reasonable control, it means that taxes must be increased at the provincial level. We are hardly any further ahead.
In some of these cases the services provided are very essential and the amounts involved in some jurisdictions are not great. For example, in Yukon, it is $27,000 for government departments and $2,000 for government agencies. In the Northwest Territories it is $42,000. However, when we consider other provinces, the amounts are very substantial. In British Columbia it is $800,000 for government departments and $220,000 for the agencies. In Alberta it is $508,000 and more than $1 million for the agencies, which effectively represent substantial tax increases. In Saskatchewan, it is $232,000 for the departments and over $700,000 for the agencies. In Ontario it is $1.2 million for departments and an insignificant amount for government agencies. In Manitoba it is $220,000 for government departments and nearly $600,000 for government agencies. In Quebec it is $983,000 for government departments. In Nova Scotia it is $94,000 for government departments and $43,000 for agencies. In New Brunswick it is $200,000 for government departments and $26,000 for agencies. There are substantial amounts for small provinces. While it is $22,000 in Prince Edward Island, I can
assure the House that they are objecting to that. In Newfoundland it is $47,000 and $27,000 respectively. Federal departments are nearly $3 million and government agencies are $300,000. We are seeing one government department charging another government department within the same jurisdiction.
The provinces know that they will have to pay these increased fees and have responded to this proposition. Let me quote some of the objections that were brought to the committee by the various departments. I will begin with the Hon. Gary Dewar of Manitoba who says:
This Bill will have the effect of imposing new costs on taxpayers and telecommunications users in this Province. We estimate the total impact to be in the neighbourhood of three quarters of a million dollars-
There has been no consultation with provincial governments before tabling this bill, even though its purpose is to effect a cost transfer to provincial agencies for services previously provided cost-free by the federal Department of Communications.
The imposition of radio licence fees on Crown agencies will create financial barriers to the installation of the most effective and flexible communications facilities for public services operated by government departments and Crown agencies.
The safety of any number of public services could be compromised by the need to limit the use of radio services in order to keep expenditures for access to the radio spectrum within budgetary limits.
Certainly, we do not want to see that. He goes on:
Of greatest concern is the fact that public emergency support services, particularly those related to fire fighting and emergency preparedness will be required to restrict access to the radio spectrum and/or tax their limited budgets to pay licence fees.
The federal Minister of Communications has made temporary commitments to limit the application of licence fee regulations to municipal services. However, this exemption is not permanent, and does not cover a number of public safety and emergency services such as fire and rescue services operated by northern communities too small to have municipal status, forest fire fighting equipment operated by provincial departments of Natural Resources, or services used by provincial Emergency Measures Organizations.
Canada will be less well prepared in times of need if agents of Her Majesty which are using the radio spectrum for safety, emergency preparedness, or rescue services are charged licence fees on the same basis as commercial undertakings.
The Minister urges reconsideration of this Bill.
There are similar letters raising similar concerns about emergency services from across the country. British Columbia noted that it is not in favour of applying the licence fees broadly across the board to government departments, agencies or municipalities where they are being used for government services or for services to the general public. They say very clearly that the fees should not apply.
Saskatchewan is also very clear on this point. They point out that subsidization in the case of telephone communications in the sparsely populated northern parts of that province will be a terrific burden in the provision of radio services.
The Associate Deputy Minister in Saskatchewan points out that while deficit reduction is an important endeavour, shifting the federal deficit onto a different level of government is not a true solution to the problem. This is particularly true when the intended solution will increase the administrative effort of both Governments. That undoubtedly will be the case.
March 12, 1987

Mr. Russell, the Minister from Newfoundland and Labrador stated:
While the financial impact of the proposed legislative amendment appears relatively small at present, I anticipate that the cost of radio licences to the Provincial Government will increase, for whatever reason, in the future.
He stated that the over-all impact of the amendment means an increased financial burden to the province.
Prince Edward Island rejects the suggestion that any part of this responsibility should be transferred to provincial Governments. They state:
The desire of the Government of Canada to reduce its deficit is understandable and fully appreciated. However, the current trend of the central government to attempt to burden the provincial governments with its financial responsibilities, whether it be through the process of rail line abandonment, innovative airport management schemes, or others, is alarming and unacceptable.
Representatives from New Brunswick appeared before the committee to state a number of concerns. They state in their brief:
The increasing trend by governments toward cost recovery of a service as a budget control measure is, in general, governed by the rationale that if a service exists for the benefit of a particular user, then the appropriateness of having that user pay in part or in whole for the cost of providing the service can be considered.
However, they point out that the user is not the Government but the people of the province, who are also taxpayers federally-
They go on to state:
In asking the province to pay radio licence fees, the federal Department of Communications has apparently identified the Government as the user of the service-
However, the greatest part of the radio licences required by the province are used to ensure the safety and well-being of its residents.
They go on to give examples of radio licences used by provincial highway patrol, the Department of Transport for highway construction and maintenance, for emergency measures and for the maintenance of forests and wildlife. They state that the Province of New Brunswick as an entity is not the particular user who benefits from the services; the residents of New Brunswick are the beneficiaries. I believe that argument is eminently reasonable.
There is strong opposition to this from my Province of Ontario. The Minister from that province states:
While I understand the government's desire to place such services on a user-pay basis, the use of radio spectrum by Ontario government users is not revenue producing. It is used to provide essential services to the public, including emergency services. The reasoning which has led you to support the exemption of municipalities from the fee requirement is fully applicable to the case of similar services provided by provincial governments.
However, they will also be in trouble because the municipal exemption is only partial and is also slipping away. He goes on to say that if the Bill is passed in its present form he would urge meetings to discuss the issues raised by the current fee schedule. He asks for delays.
In the committee I proposed an amendment which would at least partially alleviate the problems posed by this Bill. The
Radio Act
amendment I moved but was not accepted stated that there be an amendment to the Bill, that notwithstanding subsection (2):
Nothing herein provided shall be deemed to impose or authorize the imposition by regulation of a fee for any licence or certificate issued to public safety or emergency response services within Canada.
Such a provision would have lessened the impact of the Bill by saying that there would be a fee for certain of these crucial emergency services. Regrettably, however, that amendment which I believe was reasonable was ruled out of order. Therefore, the full impact of this Bill will be felt by the provinces and provincial Crown agencies.
I want to deal with what the Government will do with the extra $10 million it wishes to collect if and when this Bill is passed. If I thought the money would be used for improving post-secondary education, public broadcasting, research and development or job-creation, I suppose I might be more in favour of a tax increase, which this is essentially. However, we see that money is being spent so that companies will make profits. There is an elaborate prison for the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) riding. Other examples such as that mean we cannot expect that any additional money collected through this new tax will be put to good use for the country.
The Government has a majority and undoubtedly Bill C-3 will pass. I regret that. It means an increased burden on the provinces and, of course, no relief to the taxpayer. The $10 million the federal taxpayer does not have to pay will have to be paid by those same people who are provincial and municipal taxpayers, suggest that finding new revenues of this order and in this fashion are not, in any event, going to solve the real problems of revenue collection and the deficit. Without significant tax reform, this sort of measure is very small and is not going to remotely have the kind of impact we need. I think the Government should get on with the real problems of government. We need fair taxes and prudent use of resources for the best long-term interests of the country.
This Bill is another example of poor government and my colleagues and I intend to vote against it.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ORGANIZED CRIME ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ORGANIZED CRIME ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of appointing a Royal Commission to investigate organized crime in Canada and to include in its report observations and recommendations on:
1.	the extent to which organized crime is present and active in Canada, particularly in such activities as drug trafficking and loan-sharking;
2.	the extent to which organized crime is connected to the institutions of Canadian society;
3.	action taken by the government of other countries to investigate and curtail organized crime activity;
4.	legislation to enable the government to identify and appropriate the proceeds of organized crime;
5.	effective and appropriate punishment in instances of organized crime murder conspiracy; and
6.	possible guidelines for enforcement agencies in dealing with witnesses against organized crime.
She said: Madam Speaker, organized crime has been defined as:
Two or more persons consorting together on a continuing basis to participate in illegal activities, either directly or indirectly for gain.
This deliberate collaboration for illegal gain can develop into a self-perpetuating conspiracy that continues, despite what may happen to its original members, and that uses force and fear in its operations.
Organized crime has no ethnicity. It exists, it is pervasive, it is international in scope, and whether we know it or not, it is a fact of life. There is organized crime activity in loan-sharking, drug trafficking, robbery and extortion, activities that victimize innocent citizens. Organized crime does not exist as a separate subculture. It extends into our daily lives and the institutions of our society. The extent to which it does so is not known, and that is one of the reasons for my motion which proposes a Royal commission to investigate organized crime in Canada.
There has never been a national inquiry of this kind in Canada. There have, however, been provincial investigations. In Ontario in 1974, Judge Harry Waisberg's Royal Commission into certain sectors of the construction industry made some eye-opening revelations about the degree of corruption and organized crime involvement in Ontario's construction industry. Also in the 1970s, the reports of the Quebec crime probes extensively documented organized crime activity in that province.
The obvious conclusion, as I have said, is that organized crime is a fact of life, a force of corruption and a threat to our society. By its intrusion into other aspects of our lives, it is a threat to democracy. The issues it raises are national ones,

March 12, 1987
Organized Crime
which is why in my opinion a national investigation is called for.
Since organized crime exists to make money and buy power for those involved, it is clear that there is a good deal of money involved, many say billions, acquired illegally and outside the mainstream economy. Criminal organizations use modern financial services to conceal the illegal nature of their funds, to launder their money in other words. The increasing sophistication and the internationalization of the financial services industry make it extremely difficult to distinguish legal from illegal funds as transactions are processed in minutes through international financial networks.
In the United States in 1984, the interim report of the President's Commission on Organized Crime noted that the existence of modern financial institutions contributed to the frightening financial successes of organized crime in recent years. Without the means to launder money, organized crime could not flourish as it now does. Canadian financial institutions with their international operations are not exempt from this laundering activity. Since a great deal of the financial services industry is regulated federally, one of the questions that might be studied by a federal Royal commission would be how to remove the financial rewards of organized crime.
For example, Italian law allows for the arrest and imprisonment of organized crime conspirators as well as the confiscation of their assets. In 1970, the United States enacted the so-called RICO statute, the Racketeer-Influenced and Corrupt Organization Act, which also allows for state confiscation of the proceeds of organized crime. As a result of this law, American authorities have been able to lay charges against entire groups of organized crime conspirators as well as leaders and members of ongoing criminal conspiracies.
Last year in the United Kingdom, the British Parliament passed tough new laws to deprive convicted drug traffickers of the benefits of their illegal activities. Earlier court cases had shown that the law as it stood had no capacity to deprive offenders of the massive profits of their crimes. In 1984, the United Kingdom's Hodgson committee completed a study entitled "The Profits of Crime and Their Recovery" and recommended that the power of confiscation be made available. These are all things that a Canadian Royal commission could study to see how they might be applied in Canada.
Since organized crime operates outside the law and outside the mainstream of society, it does not welcome publicity. A Royal commission holding hearings and gathering information would create that unwelcome publicity which could possibly check the growth of organized crime, or at least prevent its operating at full capacity.
The police may become concerned that the publicity generated by a Royal commission could jeopardize their own ongoing investigations. This may be a legitimate concern which must be accommodated, but without public knowledge and support and without the necessary legislative backing, our
law enforcement authorities face an uphill battle against organized crime.
Another area of inquiry for a Royal commission might be the treatment of witnesses against organized crime. The United States has an established witness protection program to deal with these individuals who are often themselves criminals but who put themselves at risk to provide information on organized crime operations. I take seriously the argument that law enforcement authorities should not make deals with criminals. Nevertheless, since police rely on informers, we must have an examination of the matter of the ethical and legal considerations and some guidelines about how to proceed.
Another question that might be explored by a Royal commission is the question of the individual who sits at his desk and orders a murder. At this time, the House is very concerned about capital punishment and other kinds of punishment for the persons who actually commit murders but we have not been very successful in finding the kind of conspirator who is in a position to order a murder.
Perhaps the most important and valuable function of a Royal commission on organized crime would be to highlight the extent to which it has pervaded the institutions of our society and to expose its connections to the business community, the political arena, the judiciary and so on. Organized crime grows and prospers through its connections with and corruption of individuals at all levels of society, not just the wealthy and powerful. I believe that a Royal commission can make an assault on organized crime merely by exposing these connections.
The studies undertaken in Canada so far have given hints of what lies below the surface. We know there is organized crime in Canada and we know it is growing. It is a force of corruption, acting completely outside the law, interested only in expanding its own profit-making capacity at the expense of law-abiding citizens. It is a situation that cannot properly be addressed with ad hoc solutions. I believe it requires a coordinated approach on several fronts. That is why I recommend the formation of a Royal commission which would itself be part of a national response to the problem of organized crime in Canada.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ORGANIZED CRIME ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am delighted to rise to speak to the motion of my hon. colleague and friend opposite. I am always surprised and impressed by the breadth of her interest in the various topics that come before the House. As Hon. Members know, the Hon. Member is a recognized expert in financial affairs and I know of her interests in the area of criminal law. The motion she has laid before the House shows her to be thoughtful and is of much credit to her.
There is no doubt that international crime is a very serious problem. Solutions are being addressed at a global level but the question is whether we are doing enough, and whether or
March 12, 1987

not Parliament should authorize a royal commission. I am looking forward to the debate to learn the advantages and disadvantages. I know several of my colleagues have speeches they want to make on the topic. Under our rules this is fortunately a votable motion after five hours of debate. Parliament will take a collective decision. Therefore I want to commend my friend for bringing the motion forward. I regret the delay in starting today but there will be at least another four days for debate.
1 want to say a word or two about what the Government has done and is doing concerning illegal drug trafficking and organized crime. In 1985 the previous Solicitor General led the Canadian delegation to the Seventh UN Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders, held in Milan, Italy. I was fortunate to have been part of that delegation. For the first time in my life I had an opportunity to speak with elected officials and police officers from other countries in order to get a real feel for the extent of the problem. It is a bit like AIDS in that it is far more serious than people realize and has the capacity to explode exponentially. We have to do something and in fact certain things are being done.
Members of this House, and Canadians in general, will be pleased to know that Canada is in the forefront in the development of measures to attack international drug trafficking. We have also played an active role in supporting UN initiatives, including the preparation of a new convention on illicit drug trafficking. As well, we are collaborating with other economic summit countries to combat drug abuse. The Canadian delegation in Milan did an absolutely first-class job and I am sure Members will be very thankful for that contribution.
In April of 1986, Canada ratified a drug control agreement with France, the U.S. and Italy. The agreement grew out of the work done since 1970 by the quadripartite conference involving representatives of the French national police, the U.S. Bureau of Narcotics and Dangerous Drugs, and the RCMP. On March 4, 1986, Canada became a full participant with Italy in the agreement to prevent and suppress trafficking in narcotics and dangerous drugs. The agreement is in effect for five years. I think the House will applaud the fact that Canada will be hosting the next conference to be held here in Ottawa next month.
I mentioned the development of a draft UN convention on illicit drug trafficking. At the thirty-ninth session of the UN Commission on Narcotic Drugs held in February, 1985, Canada co-sponsored a resolution entitled "Initiation of the Preparation of a Draft Convention for Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances". This new convention is viewed as both a necessary and effective mechanism for implementing new initiatives to deal with illicit drug trafficking. A Canadian delegation, including representatives of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher), attended a special session of the UNCND in February, 1986, where significant progress was made in identifying the specific subjects for inclusion in the draft convention. With the exception of certain
Organized Crime
concerns relating to control of vessels and extradition, Canada generally supports the proposed measures.
A top priority for Canada for inclusion in the draft convention is a provision which would permit each member state to trace, freeze and confiscate the proceeds of drug trafficking. Canada will be introducing domestic legislation which will strengthen our ability to effectively seize and forfeit the proceeds of crime, particularly those from illicit drug trafficking. To my mind that would be an incredible step forward in controlling drug traffickers. Seizing the proceeds of crime will in itself cause the practice to dry up quickly.
Another provision providing international control of the principal precursors for the manufacture of illicit drugs, for example, those which permit the extraction of heroin from opium and cocaine from coca, would constitute a primary defence in controlling the manufacture of illicit drugs. Still another provision deals with controlled deliveries which involve the transportation of illicit drugs under controlled conditions with the knowledge and consent of the police. The main objective is to allow the offence to continue, permitting the apprehension and successful prosecution of the key principals involved rather than mere seizure of the drugs and apprehension of the couriers. Controlled deliveries represent an efficient technique which, when successful, effectively identifies major conspirators and sources at the highest level of the international drug trade.
With regard to mutual legal assistance, considerable progress has been made in the international exchange of information to combat the illicit drug trade. Emphasis will now focus on the exchange of evidence and information as it relates to the proceeds of drug trafficking. Illegally acquired assets remain virtually untouched due to inconsistencies in international and national legal systems. The UN Division on Narcotic Drugs has decided to examine possible measures to counter bank security which encourages the apparently legitimate accumulation of these illicit assets in so-called tax haven countries. Canada, meanwhile, has ratified a mutual legal assistance treaty with the U.S., and is actively negotiating similar agreements with Switzerland, the Bahamas, and other Commonwealth countries.
A further provision of the proposed convention deals with illicit traffic via commercial carriers. In most cases air carriers and shipping lines are not held accountable for baggage cargo which is being used to secretly conceal illicit drugs for shipment, or for passengers who conceal drugs. However, when it becomes evident that employees or crew are either directly involved in such activities or, because of laxness of security, allow such activity to occur, the onus must rest with the carrier.
Yet another provision deals with co-operation across frontiers. Canada agrees that international intelligence and information support is a vital activity which must be intensified in the coming years, especially concerning the international drug traffic and the conversion of profits to apparently legitimate business enterprises. Enhanced co-operation

March 12, 1987
Organized Crime
between the producing, transit and consumer nation is a priority for this Government.
The UN International Conference on Drug Abuse and Illicit Trafficking will be held in Vienna in June of this year. Members may already be aware that a Canadian, Mrs. Tamar Oppenheimer, head of the UN Division on Narcotic Drugs, is the Secretary-General of the conference. Furthermore, as an indication of the priority this Government gives to the issue, Canada will have ministerial representation at the conference. This multi-disciplinary gathering will consider such matters as the prevention and reduction of the demand for drugs, crop substitution, use of narcotics for medical purposes, forfeiture of illegal drug proceeds, the treatment and rehabilitation of drug addicts, and the enhancement of enforcement resources.
I would be remiss if I did not mention the efforts of the RCMP and other provincial and municipal police forces. The RCMP provides training to police officers for many countries every year at the Canadian police college and sends specialists to assist Commonwealth and other countries develop enforcement skills.
I see my time has expired, Madam Speaker. I will close by saying that Canada and the international community are doing much with regard to this problem. That is not to say that my friend opposite does not have a good idea. We will follow the debate with interest. A Royal commission certainly has a lot of financial and time implications and we need to hear more from Members. Perhaps the Parties would even have a position that would be helpful in coming to a decision. I thank the Hon. Member for her motion and I look forward to hearing the rest of the speakers.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ORGANIZED CRIME ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when we look at the question of organized crime and how the newspapers deal with it, we see some very startling headlines. For example, "Metro's crime gangs battle for supremacy. A three-month probe reveals organized crime in Ontario is a $2 billion industry". "Organized gangs preparing for war in bitter fight for billion-dollar turf'. "Staggering profits". "Organized crime under attack". The amounts of money suggested are really staggering. Officials say that costs limit prosecutions and the police are not able to deal with the intricacies and complexities, the number of stages of laundering, in order to deal with organized crime. Another headline reads, "Unreported tax costing billions". These are unreported taxes from elicit enterprises run by organized crime. Other headlines read, "White collar rings stay out of sight" and "Gross national rip-off". The public is the loser from the failure to pay taxes, to the intimidation of citizens, to all the direct criminal activities. Of course, the proceeds from these activities get into the grey area of so-called legal businesses which are funded and owned by organized criminals.
These are the reasons why I very much support the resolution of the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), that we have at the federal level a Royal commission to inquire into
organized crime. There have been Royal commissions and inquiries of various sorts at the provincial level on a much more limited basis. The Americans are much more actively promoting investigations of organized crime in that country. We would be smug and naive indeed to think that this problem was confined to our friends south of the border, that these activities do not take place in Canada as well. Although we are not paying as much attention to them, I believe we have a 10 per cent prorated reason to be as concerned as they are.
I come to this subject with a certain bit of a bad conscience as a sociologist. I used to study various kinds of criminal behaviour as a sociologist and academic. My own profession never paid a great deal of attention to organized crime. It is not easy to study. You cannot go out with tape recorders and questionnaires. It is not amenable to the usual academic kinds of studies. There have been the occasional book and article, usually from a journalistic approach rather than an academic one. Academics have shied away, not because they are afraid of organized crime, although perhaps we would all have a certain amount of fear if we knew the consequences. However, organized crime is obviously very successfully kept hidden. No criminal advertises in an active sense, but organized crime is kept far more hidden and is much harder to study. Even among those who have been convicted there are not large numbers of subjects for studies in the conventional sense.
Therefore, professional sociologists, psychologists, social historians and so forth have concentrated on other forms of crime. Indeed, those other forms of crime are not nearly as significant in terms of the amount of money they cost society, and probably not as significant in terms of the risk to lives of people who are intimidated and killed for not paying what is required of them in certain forms of organized crime. The fear and intimidation in organized crime is very, very serious. This is an extremely significant part of criminal life which is not being dealt with by the people who normally do conduct studies and alert the public-Parliament, and parliamentary committees-of existing problems. That source of information is not available to us. For that reason, it is even more important that we have a Royal commission which can hire some academics and very high level people who are above reproach. They will probably not be knowledgeable about organized crime, because we do not have many experts on that. Nevertheless, we could hire responsible people who would know how to conduct a commission and hire responsible staff to do the work which would put us in a much better position to address this question.
I would now like to refer to the specific proposals in the motion of the Hon. Member for Trinity which reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of appointing a Royal Commission to investigate organized crime in Canada and to include in its report observations and recommendations on:
1.	the extent to which organized crime is present and active in Canada,
particularly in such activities as drug trafficking and loan-sharking;
2.	the extent to which organized crime is connected to the institutions of
Canadian society;
March 12, 1987

3.	action taken by the governments of other countries to investigate and curtail organized crime activity;
4.	legislation to enable the government to identify and appropriate the proceeds of organized crime;
5.	effective and appropriate punishment in instances of organized crime murder conspiracy; and
6.	possible guidelines for enforcement agencies in dealing with witnesses against organized crime.
I would like to highlight the second point, "the extent to which organized crime is connected to the institutions of Canadian society", which is one of the things we do know. It is certainly clear in other countries that organized criminals like to get protection by infiltrating other social institutions. They move their money into illicit enterprises. Tracing these connections will, of course, be difficult, but it is extremely important to do this.
With regard to measures to identify and appropriate the proceeds of organized crime, some of these have already been mentioned. One suggestion that has been raised as a possible way of preventing some of the laundering of proceeds from organized crime is to make it an offence to hold a numbered bank account in another country. We would assume that anyone who did not want their money traced might be up to no good. Such a measure ought to be considered as a possibility.
The previous speaker referred a great deal to illicit drug trafficking. That is, of course, an important matter. However, I think we would be remiss in our duties if we thought that was even the largest part of organized crime. It is the myriad of activity and a movement into legal businesses which is perhaps the most devastating in terms of its impact on Canadian society.
With regard to possible guidelines for enforcement agencies in dealing with witnesses, this is a long-standing problem whenever there is an inquiry or a police case involving major figures from organized crime. The witnesses may indeed be criminals themselves and we are put in the moral dilemma of whether we want to make a deal to relieve them of their responsibility for their crimes in order to get information which may lead to more important members of the organized conspiracy. Providing adequate protection for witnesses is a very fundamental question if we are to proceed in a serious way in dealing with this issue.
In conclusion, I believe that this is an eminently sensible resolution. I urge Hon. Members in all Parties to give it support. I was pleased that the first Conservative spokesperson on this subject is at least open to the question. I hope all government Members will be open to this. More enthusiastic support may have been desirable. There is no doubt that Royal commissions are expensive. However, when we consider the enormity of the problem, the billions and billions of dollars at stake, and the number of lives which are affected by this, it seems to me that even the cost of a Royal commission could be money very well spent. I urge the Government to consider, aside from the cost of a Royal commission, the cost of not dealing with this extremely important social question. I think
Organized Crime
we must address those issues. I believe that the right thing to do is to support this resolution to establish a Royal commission to investigate organized crime.

Madam Speaker, I want to comment briefly on that part of motion M-44 under which it is proposed that the House consider the advisability of appointing a royal commission to investigate and make recommendations on the effective and appropriate punishment in instances of organized crime murder conspiracy.
First I should like to commend the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) for her interest in this matter. Surely all Hon. Members understand just how important it is for society that our laws provide appropriate sanctions with a view to punishing those who attack their fellow citizens and preventing them from committing more crimes.
As many Members of the House will know, the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1985, Bill C-18, contains an amendment to Section 423(1) of the Criminal Code, the effect of which is to increase the punishment for conspiracy to commit murder from one of imprisonment of 14 years to imprisonment for life. This term of imprisonment is subject to the normal rules with regard to parole eligibility.

Madam Speaker, there can hardly be a more serious infraction than conspiring to commit murder. To show that they acknowledged the seriousness of such a crime, parliamentarians thought that it should call for the same punishment given those found guilty of manslaughter, robbery, hostage taking, extortion.
In view of this, Madam Speaker, and although I share the sentiments of the Hon. Member for Trinity, I respectfully submit that the existing provisions of the Criminal Code concerning conspiracy to commit murder are appropriate. The longest prison term applicable, that is imprisonment for life, properly reflects the way this crime is perceived by the honest people and lets the courts take into consideration, when passing judgment, the extenuating circumstances such as change of heart and co-operation with police in order to bring to justice the other parties to the conspiracy.
Madam Speaker, as many Members know, the Law Reform Commission of Canada in its final report entitled "Recodifying criminal law", published recently, suggests in the third part of the Criminal Code draft contained in that report that in matters of conspiracy a simple rule be applied: That a guilty plea should carry only half the sentence prescribed for the crime as such.
Madam Speaker, that suggestion concerns me. Personally, 1 would not want such a clause to apply to conspiracy to commit murder, especially when organized crime is involved. As I

March 12, 1987
Organized Crime
have already said, in my opinion the present punishment seems appropriate for such an odious crime, since it is possible to take into account the degree of involvement in the crime and the extenuating or aggravating circumstances.
To conclude, Madam Speaker, I repeat that, in my opinion, the actual wording of the Criminal Code, which prescribes the most severe punishment possible, imprisonment for life, is effective and appropriate to deal with such an odious crime as conspiracy to commit murder, whether the conspiracy is by a large criminal organization or a small group.
1 thank you, Madam Speaker, for the opportunity to participate in this debate.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ORGANIZED CRIME ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) for her interest in matters relating to the administration of justice, especially dealing with organized crime in Canada. I believe we have seen an increase in this regard which has taken place essentially since the end of World War II. It should also be pointed out that many of us do not realize that we are dealing with organized crime very innocently when many of the things we purchase today may have resulted from organized crime. Certainly it is obvious that young people who today are involved with drugs and other things are very much contributing to the increase of organized crime.
I want to take a few minutes to discuss the specific aspect of the Member's motion which relates to the development of legislation to enable the Government to identify and appropriate the proceeds of crime. There is no question that the financial rewards from criminal activity, especially drug trafficking, are substantial. Because of the underground nature of the activity, it is difficult to estimate the exact dollar figure with any degree of accuracy. A Member who spoke previously suggested that the figure is possibly $2 billion in Ontario. No one can guess for sure the exact amount involved in organized crime, but it is certainly substantial.
In addition to the profit, there is the added social cost of law enforcement and health and education programs related to drug abuse. There is also the hidden cost of lost productivity on the job due to drug use. Anyone who visits a criminal court will certainly see the effect that drugs are having on our community, leading to such things as theft, prostitution and even murder.
A few years ago I had an opportunity to participate in a jury trial in which drugs were involved in a murder. When one begins to delve into those matters, one can see the effect that organized crime is having on our society. The costs to the community are as substantial as the profits from crime. These profits, which represent a tragic cost to Canadian society, are then used to fund other criminal activities such as graft, theft, pornography and prostitution. There is also the laundering effects of these profits into real estate or other businesses.
If the police are able to make a case that results in the imposition of a jail sentence for one of these offenders, the
criminal empire continues to flourish in the hands of his associates who await his eventual release from prison. He only has to wait the situation out before he is back on the street and already set up in business. The deterrent aspect of the sentence is completely lost when the offender knows that upon his being released he can continue that opulent life style that his criminal career has created for him.
In partnership with the provinces, a detailed analysis of organized crime was completed in June, 1983. Included in the recommendations of that report was a legislative scheme to trace, seize and confiscate the fruits of crime. Because there is also a need to reduce the demand for illicit drugs, it is obvious that a program of education is required in conjunction with an attack on the criminal element supplying the product.
In direct response to this problem, the Government announced in the Throne Speech the need to take effective action against the traffic in illicit drugs, as well as to develop a national drug strategy. Virtually all other western countries have legislation providing for the confiscation of the fruits of crime. No country is immune from this monstrous problem. I would anticipate from the words of the Speech from the Throne that the Government will be dealing with this specific aspect of the Member's motion.
Experience has shown that there is a need to freeze assets at the pre-trial stage, so that they will be available for confiscation upon conviction. This may be done by means of a court authorized system of seizure or restraint orders, with the option to appoint an interim manager, if required. Third party interests could be protected by a system of court procedures to determine any innocent interest that should be exempted from the confiscation scheme. What would be expected is a workable mechanism to confiscate criminal assets without sacrificing any innocent parties and always reflecting due process.
The previous Government attempted to pass legislation relating to both the proceeds of crime and instruments of crime. The inclusion of instruments such as businesses that were only minimally tainted by the infusion of criminal funds was perceived as Draconian and I would expect that any initiative entertained by this Government would be limited to only the proceeds of crime.
There is no question that the motivation of the Hon. Member in relation to the presentation of this motion is completely based on very good faith. However, in light of the clear commitment of the Government, as detailed in the Speech from the Throne, it is clear that action in this area will be forthcoming, and that is obvious from other initiatives that have been presented to the House in fulfilment of our promises to the Canadian people.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, before commenting the motion presented by the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), I would like to congratulate her for drawing the attention of this House to the issue of organized crime.
March 12, 1987

However, I fear that a Royal Commission of Inquiry on this matter would have the opposite effect to that desired. Some Canadians, probably influenced by the American medias, have greatly exagerated ideas about the extent of organized crime in Canada and its presence in our social, economic and political institutions.
I am certainly not trying to minimize the threat of organized crime in Canada, especially in the illegal drug traffic. However, I am convinced that the action taken by all levels of government in Canada to repress organized crime are increasingly effective, and I am happy to note that there is no indication that organized crime is endemic in Canadian institutions.
In my opinion, there is really no need to ask a royal commission to examine this matter.
Royal commissions are very costly, and since their rules of evidence are not as stringent as those of the Canadian courts and the evidence brought before them cannot be used in criminal proceedings, it is not very useful for law enforcement purposes.
In addition, Madam Speaker, creating a royal commission would probably worry Canadians needlessly by giving the impression that our police forces and courts are not fighting properly against organized crime.
Moreover, I fear that a royal commission would divert attention and resources from existing initiatives in the area of information and law enforcement and eventually delay investigations and legal proceedings in serious cases.
Madam Speaker, the royal commission which is proposed would run the risk of delaying initiatives at the national and international level in the fight against organized crime.
As I have mentioned before, federal, provincial and municipal authorities are already committed to this task. The existing national intelligence systems are upgraded continuously and police forces pool their knowledge, experience and ability in joint operations aimed at the big names in organized crime.
Important institutions such as Canadian banks are seeking the best possible means to protect themselves from laundered money.
As for the Federal and Provincial Governments, they are looking ever more seriously at legislation other than the Criminal Code which could help prevent or fight organized crime.
Both at the federal and provincial levels, police officers are being better trained and given the knowledge and skills required to detect organized criminal activity and to gather the necessary evidence for successful prosecution in important
cases.
However, these efforts generally go unseen and the media make no mention of them. In Canada, particularly, we have a
Organized Crime
tendency to say little about what we do and to be more discreet than our American neighbours.
In my opinion, Madam Speaker, the law enforcement methods used by the Canadian authorities in their fight against organized crime are highly efficient. Efforts and resources are coordinated and the various jurisdictions cooperate to prevent and expose illegal activities, to conduct investigations and to prosecute offenders. In other respects, Canadian authorities share a particular concern for the rights of people who unknowingly become accomplices.
Enforcement policies and activities are aimed at maintaining the confidence of Canadians in the integrity of our social, political and economic institutions, which are the main forces that stand against the corruption generated by organized crime.
Police authorities, the courts and other Canadian enforcement agencies are the watchdogs of that integrity, representing as they do our first line of defence against organized crime.
It has been said that the importance of the underworld in a society is an indication of the integrity and ethics of its Government and business institutions. We must therefore support policies and programs ensuring that Canada never will be a country where the underworld can take root. And that goal requires that the various governments and enforcement agencies be on a constant watch.
The Government appreciates the genuine concern of the Hon. Member about organized crime. However, the Government of Canada is co-operating with the provinces in intensifying enforcement efforts, and a royal commission of inquiry would add very little to the tools already in place or being developed.
Preferably, Madam Speaker, this House should support and encourage the Canadian Government and the provinces in their enforcement initiatives, and enact rapidly any legislation aimed at increasing the effectiveness of the law against organized crime.
I am aware, Madam Speaker, that the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Trinity reflects a serious concern about the extent of organized crimes in Canada and the weakness of measures to promote enforcement. But I want to assure her that members of the police forces and other dedicated experts in the area of penal justice are showing a high degree of competence in addressing this problem. The Government is relying on them, and they deserve the support of all Hon. Members and Canadians in general.
I do not feel therefore that the setting up of a royal commission would be in the interests of Canadians or would help our fight against organized crime.

Madam Speaker, I am very pleased indeed for this opportunity to speak to the

March 12, 1987
Adjournment Debate
motion, I wish to thank the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) for drawing to the attention of the House this very important matter. My Government is very much aware of the problems of organized crime. My colleagues have already discussed many of the initiatives the Government has taken to combat organized crime in terms of improved legislation, enhanced resources, improved systems of collecting, analysing and disseminating intelligence on organized crime and, indeed, with new arrangements with foreign governments to help solve this very pressing problem.
In presenting this motion, the Hon. Member proposed that one of the matters the Royal commission would investigate is the matter of witnesses against organized crime. In this connection, I am pleased to report that the matter is currently being examined by the Ministry of the Solicitor General in collaboration with provincial Ministers and other federal Ministers concerned with law enforcement. I believe we would all agree that witness protection is part and parcel of a serious commitment on the part of the Government and law enforcement agencies to forcefully pursue organized criminal activities.
Some Hon. Members may be aware that in the United States the federal Government instituted a witness protection program aimed at organized crime which is administered by the U.S. Marshalls Service. The need for a wide ranging formal program in the United States is, of course, based on the magnitude of the organized crime problem there. Fortunately, we are not yet faced with a problem of similar magnitude in Canada. As Members are aware, the administration of justice is a provincial responsibility. As a consequence, the majority of witnesses requiring protection, relocation and a new identity are the responsibility of provincial authorities. The federal Government, through the RCMP and other federal departments, does however provide assistance to provincial officials in the form of documentation required for the witness to establish a new identity, usually in a new location in a new town. The RCMP also assists other police forces in other aspects of witness protection.
These flexible arrangements which provide for witness protection has worked in a generally satisfactory way at meeting the Canadian needs over the years.

subtopic: DISASTERS-CHERNOBYL NUCLEAR ACCIDENT-EFFECT ON CARIBOU IN LABRADOR AND QUEBEC. (B) ABILITY TO MONITOR RADIOACTIVE CONTAMINATION
DISASTERS-CHERNOBYL NUCLEAR ACCIDENT-EFFECT ON CARIBOU IN LABRADOR AND QUEBEC. (B) ABILITY TO MONITOR RADIOACTIVE CONTAMINATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to pursue a question I asked of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) on December 3, as well as my follow-up letter to him on January 22, relating to the impact of the Chernobyl nuclear accident on Canada.
On December 3 I asked the Minister to make public information on what monitoring took place in Canada following Chernobyl, where the monitoring took place, what was monitored and what the result was in terms of radioactive contamination. In response to my question the Minister indicated a willingness to make a statement to this House, or otherwise provide the House and the Canadian public with further information on the impact of Chernobyl on Canada.
On December 11 the Minister tabled a document entitled "The Impact of the Chernobyl Nuclear Accident on Canada". Unfortunately, this document fell far short of the type of detailed information I was seeking when I asked my question on December 3. As a result, I wrote to the Minister on January 22 expressing my dissatisfaction with the report and again asking him to table a comprehensive statement on the radioactive contamination of the Canadian environment in the days and weeks after Chernobyl. To date, the Minister has yet to respond to my request. I would like to take this opportunity to again put on the record why I feel it is so important that the Government provide the House and all Canadians with the type of detailed information I requested.
To begin, the document the Minister tabled on December 11 states that 28 monitoring stations at airports across Canada were activated shortly after the Chernobyl nuclear accident. I point out to the Government that this network is far less comprehensive than the 33 monitoring stations activated in Sweden, a country 22 times smaller than Canada. In addition, the document the Minister tabled in December leads one to conclude that only air and precipitation samples were collected at the 28 monitoring stations in question at or near ground level, whereas Sweden, for example, also collected air samples at different altitudes through the use of aircraft, as well as plant samples. The report also fails to give any indication of the sophistication of the equipment the Government uses to monitor radioactive fall-out or whether the Government availed itself of the sophisticated monitoring equipment that exists at several Canadian universities and private facilities.
Most important, the report tabled by the Minister does not indicate what isotopes the Canadian monitoring stations were
March 12, 1987

looking for, what they discovered, where, and in what quantities. For example, the report refers to radiation doses in microsieverts but fails to identify the individual isotope levels detected or the methodology used to calculate the doses quoted in the report.
The Government's estimates of the long-term effects of Chernobyl are equally suspect because the report again fails to identify the individual isotope levels detected, and also fails to detail which cumulative dose commitments and which international standards were employed to calculate the risk assessment outlined in the report, thereby seriously undermining the credibility of the Government's projection that there will be less than one Canadian cancer fatality as a result of Chernobyl. As a case in point, Dr. Rosalie Bertell, last year's winner of the Alternate Nobel Peace Prize, estimates that the number of Canadian cancers that could be expected as a result of Chernobyl may actually be anywhere from 1 to 24, with 3 to 9 cancers being the most probable.
Dr. Bertell also noted that the Government has not published projections on the reproductive problems that might be expected from Chernobyl, such as genetic diseases, embryonic, foetal, or infant losses, mild mutations, lower birth weights or growth retardation, which she estimates could be anywhere from 25 to 169 cases.
Similarly, the Government's claim that only 12 of 300 samples of imported food were rejected after Chernobyl is somewhat meaningless without detailed information on what isotopes the inspectors were looking for, what monitoring techniques, or what doses were judged to be acceptable or unacceptable.
I could go on, Madam Speaker, but I hope that I have made my point that it is essential that Canadians be provided with all known information on Chernobyl in order to analyse and reflect on the true impact of the accident on ourselves and on our environment.
This information is important for another reason. It now appears probable that some of the radiation detected over Canada in the wake of the Chernobyl accident did not come from Chernobyl, but rather from the venting of radiation trapped underground as a result of the "Mighty Oak" nuclear bomb blast that took place at the Nevada nuclear test sites on April 10, 1986, 16 days prior to the incident at Chernobyl. Both the United States Department of Energy, and the United States Environmental Protection Agency have confirmed that venting of radiation trapped underground as a result of this test occurred shortly before, and in particular, after Chernobyl. Appropriate monitoring equipment can differentiate between radiation from a bomb blast and radiation from a nuclear reactor accident. But again the Government's failure to release the full results of its post-Chernobyl monitoring prevent adequate public analysis and reflection on the true risks of Chernobyl, or the apparently never-ending string of
Adjournment Debate
nuclear tests being conducted by the United States in our shared North American environment.
I should also point out that if some of the fall-out detected in Canada after Chernobyl did come from the "Mighty Oak" bomb blast in the United States, that bomb blast-not to mention many others before it-would be in direct violation of the 1963 Nuclear Test Ban Treaty which forbids any nuclear weapons tests that would impact on any territory outside of the jurisdiction of the country conducting the test.
As you may know, Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), and myself, are currently travelling across the country to listen to ordinary Canadians and experts alike as part of the NDP inquiry into the nuclear fuel cycle in Canada. These hearings have been most productive to date, and we hope to publish a report some time during the fall of this year. During our hearings, considerable concern has been raised about Canada's ability to monitor radioactive fall-out.
We have also heard a lot about excessive secrecy when it comes to nuclear issues in Canada. One could argue that the report that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) tabled on December 11, and the Government's apparent continued unwillingness to release further details on the impact of Chernobyl on Canada, merely confirm both these concerns. Or are we to believe, which might even be more distressing, that the Government does not have this type of information? Therefore, Canadians ought to be doubly concerned about what the Government was doing, or not doing, in the days and weeks following the Chernobyl accident.
I see that the Minister is in the House, presumably to answer my question, and I wish to say I am happy that the Minister has chosen to respond to my statement this afternoon. I hope he will be more forthcoming in what he has to say to the House at this time.
