subtopic: DISASTERS-CHERNOBYL NUCLEAR ACCIDENT-EFFECT ON CARIBOU IN LABRADOR AND QUEBEC. (B) ABILITY TO MONITOR RADIOACTIVE CONTAMINATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the first point I wish to make to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) and all Canadians is that all information that Canada has and that the Radiation Centre has that has been available from universities and private laboratories I have been willing to make public, both immediately after Chernobyl and during the following months when there was great interest in Chernobyl as well as the present.
I wish to convey very directly that there is nothing that we are hiding in terms of information. As I have previously stated, if there is additional information that can be made available, I will make that available.
Second, I wish to discuss the matter of Canadian standards relative to international standards. We have checked that very carefully with various international agencies and as recently as during the parliamentary break, on my visit to Vienna I met with representatives of the International Atomic Energy Agency, namely, Dr. Blix from Sweden and Professor Konstin-tinov from the Soviet Union. We looked at what took place at

March 12, 1987
Adjournment Debate
the meetings in Vienna relative to the information that came forward from Chernobyl. The Soviets, as we know, had been very secretive about the information initially. That information came forward to some degree at the hearings in Vienna during the special convention of the IAEA. That information is available as well, Madam Speaker. Because of this issue being so sensitive, it is important to stress that we have made all information available that is known to us, both nationally and internationally. If there is more information, we will also make that available.
As to the second part of the question relating to the effect of Chernobyl on the food cycle, the caribou-human food chain, I want to tell Members and Canadians that we have been looking at that matter very seriously. A few weeks ago I had an opportunity to discuss this with health officials at Frobisher Bay. By all measurements the radioactivity measured in the Arctic, post-Chernobyl, was considerably lower than any radiation that, for example, had been measured in the 1960s at the height of the atomic blasts at that time-I am not using it as a standard that we are better off than in the 1960s and therefore everything is fine, but we have to take comparisons here-and the chance of death from radioactivity of even one caribou is so small as to be virtually zero.
As well, we have received reports from Scandinavian countries on the contamination of reindeer herds and their being unfit for human consumption. It should be noted that there are no reports of death of caribou even though their exposure to radiation was higher than that received in Canada. However, to protect northern residents, meat samples from at least 30 caribou from the main herds in the Territories have been collected by the Canadian Wildlife Service. We are doing that in co-operation with Health and Welfare in co-operation with Health and Welfare. This sampling program will be repeated this spring. The departments will make these samples available along with all information. According to all information we have, both the caribou, that is the food chain, and Canadians in the North and elsewhere have been fully protected and fully informed on everything flowing from Chernobyl, and we will continue that action.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES-(A) REQUEST THAT MINISTER BE MORE PRECISE (B) FUTURE OF PUBLIC SERVANTS AND FAMILIES

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES-(A) REQUEST THAT MINISTER BE MORE PRECISE (B) FUTURE OF PUBLIC SERVANTS AND FAMILIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to shed some light on a question that has aroused the concern of some 1,300 federal public servants at the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources who work for the Surveys and Mapping Branch and the Centre for Remote Sensing, and also at the Canadian Hydrographic Service of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans.
Madam Speaker, this Government which was supposed to be straightforward in its dealings has managed to scare everyone
through sheer incompetence. If we look back on what happened five or six days ago, we get a very clear picture of how this Government managed to complicate a situation that should have been very straightforward.
Last Friday on March 5, the employees' union at Energy, Mines and Resources issued a press release announcing that mapping, remote sensing and hydrographic services would be turned over, privatized if you prefer, to Lavalin, a world-class engineering firm.
The press release tells us that various Ministers were consulted and gave contradictory versions of the story. This was not surprising, nor was it particularly reassuring for the employees. The press release also tells us that the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines (Mr. Merrithew) would deny these rumours in the House very shortly. When we ask the Minister of State for privatization (Mrs. McDougall) to make a few comments on this possibility of privatization she denies it but goes on to say that negotiations are under way. For his part, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) says there were no real negotiations, but here are his own words as reported on page 3953 of Hansard:
Quite frankly, we had some purely exploratory talks-
Good. Last Friday the Minister of Mines told me it was not in the strict sense of the word privatization.
But as always with this Government they all have something to say, but not to one another, with the result that people become confused and concerned. They play with the sentiments and security of people.
Madam Speaker, what do you think is the reaction of an employee who does not know whether he will be privatized, whether his service and his job will still be there? Will he have to move? Madam Speaker, it is difficult to explain the anguish felt by certain employees faced with such a possibility. This is a serious matter, we are not talking about just any company. Lavalin, a major international firm, and Bell Canada, one of our largest companies, are invited by Treasury Board officials to get together to discuss the proposed privatization of what we consider to be essential services-mapping, remote sensing and hydrography.
Morale among public servants is low, and I can understand why. Because Government representatives seem to be talking at cross purposes, public servants have no idea what to expect next and they are very, very confused.
Faced with such confusion, on Monday March 6 the President of the Treasury Board in turn issues a press release to shed light on the whole situation.
On page 3953 of Hansard for March 9, we find the reply given by the Minister to the effect that the Government was having exploratory talks with several companies to discuss the make or buy policy. There have been no negotiations or contracts or any attempts in this respect. There have never been any attempts to engage in an exercise of this kind, as stated in the Minister's press release.
March 12, 1987

This is even more confusing, Madam Speaker. On one hand, there are negotiations and talks. Three meetings were held, in October, November and December, but I repeat that, according to the Minister, there have been no negotiations. My God, what are those people doing? If they are talking, it must be about something interesting. Either they are speaking about the possibility of having serious exchanges, or else they are talking just for the fun of it. I do not think that Lavalin would want to waste its time with public servants or departmental officials who do not know what they have to offer.
On Monday, Lavalin published a press release in which its president, Mr. Lamarre, confirmed the facts as follows:
"In accordance with its make or buy policy, the Treasury Board had initiated discussions with its firm and Bell Canada-" and this is textual "-to explore the terms for privatizing certain Government services in the field of cartography."
That is quite clear. Lavalin says that there have been negotiations. On the other hand, the Minister says that there have been no negotiations and wonders why the Opposition and the public servants are so excited. The facts are quite clear. The Government does not know where it is going.
In the same press release, Lavalin said: "It is already a known fact that Lavalin and Bel! Canada have recently joined forces to put together a business specialized in the management of mapping-related information, including surveying and cartography. By uniting the efforts of this new business to those of federal agencies which already operate competently in this field, Canada could play a frontline role in the development of geomatics".
As I was saying, Madam Speaker, Lavalin is a serious business which does not generally find it amusing to take the public for a ride just for publicity purposes. It does not need it. Mr. Lamarre is a serious man who has no need to advertise or to publish press releases making silly statements. Today, the Ministers have confirmed in the House that the Surveys and Mapping Branch, the Canada Centre for Remote Sensing and the Canadian Hydrographic Service are not for sale. I think that was definitely the conclusion we could draw from the answers given by the Minister of State responsible for privatization and by the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines. Those are the facts, and in that case, Lavalin has been wasting its time. It is high time this Government made up its mind where it is going, and I hope that the Hon. Member or the Minister is going to tell me the matter is closed and mapping will not be privatized.

speakeroldname: Mr. Michel Champagne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES-(A) REQUEST THAT MINISTER BE MORE PRECISE (B) FUTURE OF PUBLIC SERVANTS AND FAMILIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, thank goodness we are getting to the end of the adjournment debate, because if we listen to the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) when he starts talking about where the Government is going, I think we could also ask him where his party is going. We had a good example of this yesterday. He should listen to
Adjournment Debate
what I have to say and maybe he won't have to ask those questions anymore.
The example that occurred to me was the vote on the Cruise missile. They can't even agree in their own caucus, and in that case I wonder why he feels he is in a position to judge whether we can or cannot agree.
Madam Speaker, I think it is obvious, and I recall what was said by the Member for Ottawa-Vanier, that exploring possibilities does not mean one is going to sell. People who don't understand that are certainly lacking in judgment. I think that looking at our institutions and our departments and seeing whether we could not make their operations more efficient is one of the obligations we have as a responsible Government. Madam Speaker, bearing that in mind, I think we can look to the future with optimism and consider setting up mechanisms that will benefit all Canadians. That is what we are looking at, that is what we want to achieve, and that is what the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines (Mr. Merrithew), the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) and the Minister of State for Privatization (Mrs. McDougall) have said.
Madam Speaker, I fail to understand why the Opposition insists on making words say what they are not supposed to say, because there is a big difference between exploring and selling. We can make projections, we can analyze certain things, but that does not mean at all that we are going to sell. It means that we want to make certain improvements, look at the situation as it is now and perhaps as it should have been if the Liberals had lived up to their election promises to locate the cartography sector in Sherbrooke. Madam Speaker, the Liberals campaigned on this issue in two or three elections and failed to do anything, but now that they are on the Opposition benches they still have no idea where they are going yet are quite prepared to tell us how we should be managing public affairs. Madam Speaker, they should look at the way we reduced the deficit, they should look at the way we revived the economy over the past three years. They should realize that this Government can give Canadians an opportunity to rejoin the labour force, to have confidence in the economy, to look forward to a bright future. Once they have done that we will be in a position to respond to sensible questions from another Party, like the Opposition Party.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, I want to say that both the Minister of State (Forestry and Mines), who is responsible for the Surveys and Mapping Branch, and the President of the Treasury Board have said that there is no plan to sell or privatize the branch, the Canada Centre for Remote Sensing or the Canadian Hydrographic Service, and any statement to the contrary would simply be false.
Madam Speaker, I hope these few comments are sufficiently clear and specific.

March 12, 1987
Adjournment Debate

subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-PUBLIC TENDERS-OPPORTUNITY TO AMEND LAW AND REGULATIONS TO ELIMINATE POSSIBLE CONFLICT OF INTEREST AND CORRUPTION-GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) CANADA ELECTIONS ACT-REQUEST FOR AMENDMENTS TO BAN CORPORATE DONATIONS TO POLITICAL PARTIES

THE ADMINISTRATION-PUBLIC TENDERS-OPPORTUNITY TO AMEND LAW AND REGULATIONS TO ELIMINATE POSSIBLE CONFLICT OF INTEREST AND CORRUPTION-GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) CANADA ELECTIONS ACT-REQUEST FOR AMENDMENTS TO BAN CORPORATE DONATIONS TO POLITICAL PARTIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canadians are very tired of all the scandals, corruption, hints of conflict of interest, resignations and investigations. Whether it be government contracts, legal services, or renting buildings, Canadians want to see a clean system and a Government they can be proud of.
I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) if he would set up a fair system of public tendering. I do not think many Canadians realize how many loopholes there are in our public tendering system. People think there is an official process and companies which want to sell goods or services to the Government make an offer which is examined impartially by civil servants and the lowest bidder which fulfils the necessary qualifications gets the work. Of course, many contracts are not covered in that fashion. We have government contract regulations and then a vast assortment of exceptions where the Minister can proceed without going through the tendering system.
When I raised this issue with the Prime Minister, he denied there was a problem. All he said was if I had a specific case then I should complain about that. That is not what I was talking about. No doubt the police can deal with a specific case or a specific crime. What I am talking about is the need to have a system that Canadians know is fair.
I think it is scandalous to hear that the Minister of Supply and Services (Mrs. Vezina) lets certain MPs know about contracts which are coming up so that the MP can go around to friends or companies, possibly those who gave the MP financial contributions in the last election, and suggest there is a chance they can get some government business. I do not think MPs should be in that business. That is what we have a Public Service for. We should have impartial officials dealing with these contracts for everything other than purely trivial amounts. We do not want to call for a public tender every time we buy a pencil or eraser, but for any serious amount of contracting there should be a fair system so people will know where they stand and so the decisions will be made by public servants. We do not have that.
One constructive proposal which I made, because I think Canadians want constructive solutions to this, is that we try to stem the incentive which corporations have to use improper methods of getting contracts by stopping corporate donations to political parties. This is a serious suggestion. It was pooh-poohed by the Prime Minister. He did not want to consider it
at all. The answer we get to that is that the NDP gets donations from unions and is it not, therefore, in the same boat as the Liberals and Conservatives. We are not in the same boat at all. Unions are not out to get government contracts. They are not selling goods and services and trying to make a profit for their shareholders. It is quite a different situation. The opportunity for corruption just is not there.
In Quebec unions, as corporations, are not permitted to make campaign donations. It is one of the legacies of Rene Levesque and the Parti Quebecois that they have cleaned up that system in Quebec. They ought to be very proud of that. I only hope that we will follow suit at the federal level and ensure that we have at least as good a system for federal donations.
In fact, both the Conservatives and Liberals get enormous amounts of money from private corporations. In 1984, our last election year, the Conservatives raised S22 million; the Liberals, $11.8 million; and the NDP was a little behind that at $10.5 million. Half of the funds raised by the Conservatives and Liberals came from corporations. That is a substantial amount of money. In short, the Conservative Party raised more money from corporations than the New Democratic Party raised from individuals and unions combined.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) is misleading people when he says that the New Democratic Party gets most of its money from unions. That is simply not true. We get between 10 and 20 per cent depending upon the year and the jurisdiction. We depend overwhelmingly on individual donations. I am sure people would be prepared to consider whether unions should be making contributions. I do not think they are in the same boat as corporations because they are not out to make profits, but in order to have a decent system that is something which could be considered.
As well as corporate donations going to political Parties at the national level, they also go to local candidates in the Conservative and Liberal Parties. In the case of the Hon. Member for Manicouagan, who became the Prime Minister after the election, corporate donations to his riding association in that election year amounted to $58,0000. That was far beyond the spending limit. In the case of the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) corporate donations in 1984 were $64,000 although his spending limit was $24,000. It is clear that corporations think they are betting on the winner and that it will do them some good.
I do not think Canadians want that kind of system. I think Canadians were glad to see the end of the bad old days when voters were paid a bottle of rum for their vote and every time there was an election the civil servants from the previous government were thrown out and replaced with people from the Party in power. I am proud of the role that Tommy Douglas and the CCF in Saskatchewan played in cleaning that province up from political corruption and patronage. They instituted a merit principle in the civil service and a public tendering system which did not grant contracts to friends or contributors to the Party in power. They did not take corporate
March 12, 1987

donations so there was no incentive for corporations to try to buy influence by making political donations. That system worked. They got very good value for their money. They cleaned up the system. We know that they even managed to reduce the deficit while providing excellent services. I do think it possible, Madam Speaker, and I would hope that we could have a system in Canada which is fair and clean. That is what Canadians want.
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of Supply and Services):
subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-PUBLIC TENDERS-OPPORTUNITY TO AMEND LAW AND REGULATIONS TO ELIMINATE POSSIBLE CONFLICT OF INTEREST AND CORRUPTION-GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) CANADA ELECTIONS ACT-REQUEST FOR AMENDMENTS TO BAN CORPORATE DONATIONS TO POLITICAL PARTIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am grateful for this opportunity to talk about the federal Government contract award system.
In recent weeks, Madam Speaker, Members of the Opposition have been saying just about anything on this question without even going to the trouble of seeking a minimum of information on the subject, and especially without taking time to think about it.
Let us be frank. Every year my Department awards in excess of 350,000 contracts for goods and services worth $7 billion. For the whole federal administration, we are talking about roughly 400,000 contracts a year. So how many of these have caused problems? A minimum number, Madam Speaker.
Early in January, the Opposition tried to embarrass the Government with what has been dubbed the Oerlikon Affair. 1 would like my colleague to show some objectivity.
When he was informed of certain disturbing aspects of a land purchase by the Oerlikon company, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) asked for the resignation of a Cabinet Minister and for an investigation by the RCMP. This decision clearly demonstrates that he has no intention of making allowances as far as the confidential nature of Government transactions is concerned.
As for the bidding process and the evaluation of the bids received, to my knowledge, no one has questioned the integrity of this process. The contract for the low altitude defence system has indeed been granted to the most deserving supplier. If my colleague has any information to the contrary, I invite
Adjournment Debate
her, as the Prime Minister has already done, to communicate this information to the House.
Madam Speaker, our contracting system is highly regulated, for the very purpose of avoiding any irregularity. All purchasing agents of my department have on their shelves a dozen volumes of regulations and procedures to be followed for each type of acquisition. These books, which are quite heavy, represent all the institutional wisdom accumulated by my Department in its 18 years of existence and by the Department of Defence Production during the 40 years before that. These volumes reflect our constant efforts to act fairly and impartially in our relations with Government suppliers.
One final remark, as Minister of Supply and Services. I am convinced that the State is not a purchaser like any other. As a Government, we must see to it that our purchasing policies are absolutely consistent with our social and economic objectives. Would my hon. colleague who is greatly aware of the need to advance the status of women blame me, for instance, for having ordered a new call for tenders because some companies had disregarded our job equity program?
Madam Speaker, I will see to it that our purchasing policies are consistent with our national goals. If my hon. friend considers this approach as a form of political interference, I deeply regret it.
The Hon. Member has recommended that the Government ban corporate donations to political parties. In this regard, the Prime Minister was most clear in his reply. He said that the Government would consider the Hon. Member's suggestion.
This being said, I sincerely deplore her statement that contributions to political party foster corruption. Again, I urge her to provide us with one single example so we can make sure that justice is done.
